speechtext:
I do not know. I
know that the Union government did not do much good and I entertain grave doubts as to whether a union of the railways would be satisfactory. I could not answer that question [Mr. McMurray.l
offhand; it is altogether too large to discus at the moment. But I do object to this legislation. It seems to me to be a patchwork attempt at compromise and it will meet with nothing but protest from the people of the west. It is not fair to British Columbia, and being unfair to that province it must in consequence be unfair to a large section of the western prairies. Why could not the western section of Canada have been taken into consultation and a quid pro quo worked out along lines satisfactory to everyone? This present legislation is not satisfactory, and I make the statement fully appreciating the difficult position in which the minister finds himself. Indeed, no one appreciates more than I do the difficulties of the Minister of Railways; I doubt if any man has ever held that portfolio in Canada under similar conditions and with problems so serious to solve. I do believe however that the only solution for our railway problems is to have more industrious people living in the country, people of simple habits, people of real thrift, who will settle along the lines of railway, producing those commodities which the world requires.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
I have a good deal of
sympathy with the government in its attempt to solve the intricate and complicated problem of freight rates. The Speech from the Throne at the beginning of the session intimated that we were to have an adjustment of freight rates which would equalize rates between provinces. I maintain that this is exactly what the present bill does not propose to do, although I notice that in the order in council the same intimation was made. Thi3 bill does not propose to equalize freight rates as between provinces, and personally that is my sole reason for opposing it. We in the west have been compelled all through the history of the prairie provinces to pay very much higher rates than are collected in eastern Canada, and an equalization between all the provinces would certainly be in our interests, and it would appear to be just and right in the interests of Canada as a whole. It apparently is assumed in eastern Canada, judging by the expressions of opinion that appear in the press and which one hears privately, that the west has some particular boon conferred upon it by the Crowsnest rates. The commodity rates referred to from eastern to western Canada are however still higher than the rates for similar commodities and equal distances in effect in eastern Canada. Why therefore should it be considered that the Crowsnest rates are a boon to that part of the country? In the first place, the Crowsnest

Railway Freight Rates
rates were not regular rates; they were not rates that were put into effect, but were simply maximum rates. And in the agreement made between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Dominion government at that time, statutory maximum rates were fixed above which the regular rates could not at any time go. These rate9, for a long period of years, from 1898 to 1918, weire still higher than the regular rates charged by the railways, so that in all that period we got no benefit whatever from the Crowsnest agreement; and so soon a3 we might have received some benefit from it, so soon as the scale of railway rates began to rise in the country, as it did during the war, the Crowsnest pass rates were set aside for a period of three years. The rates on grain and flour were permitted to come into effect again on July 6, 1922, and from that . period on we have received some definite benefit. But that is the first time in all the history of the west that we' have derived any advantage whatever from the Crowsnest pass rates. The commodity rates from eastern Canada to the prairies became effective on July 7, 1924, and we received some benefit from these rates up to October 29 of the same year, a period of only three months; for after that date these rates were set aside by order of the railway commission. The government over-ruled that order however, to make the rates effective on December 25 last and since that time these rates have been in force and we have been receiving some benefit. But the point I want to make is that in all the twenty-eight years that the Crowsnest rates have been in effect we have benefited only during a few months. The hon. member (Mr. McCrea) speaking last night made the statement that on July 6, 1922 we received reductions amounting to about thirty-five per cent in some of our freight schedules while in eastern Canada they received reductions amounting to only six per cent. But the hon. member did not tell the House that this was only a partial removal of the discrimination which for many years had existed against western Canada. The hon. gentleman went on to quote a few figures and attempted to prove that almost all the taxes were paid by the two central provinces. In that connection he submitted some very interesting figures. For instance, he pointed out that Prince Edward Island contributed only 26i cents per head of the revenues of the Dominion while Quebec contributed $52.24 and Ontario $52.21. On the other hand, he stated, Manitoba contributed $27, Saskatchewan only $3.76 and Alberta only $8.67.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: What about British Columbia?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: I have not the figures of that province.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Its contribution is $45.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: The hon. member failed to draw a distinction between those who paid the taxes and the point at which the taxes were paid. To be fair to the Maritime provinces, let me take the case of Prince Edward Island. Prince Edward Island is a purely rural province, there being nothing worthy of the name of a manufacturing establishment in the whole island; in fact, the majority of the retailers buy their goods from wholesalers resident outside of the province. The wholesaler in St. John or Halifax buying a shipment of goods on which he pays the duty, wholesales these goods to retailers in Prince Edward Island. Now, surely there is no hon. gentleman who would attempt to prove that the duty was all paid either by St. John or Halifax; the duty is passed on to the consumer in Prince Edward Island. And that is the condition in the prairies. We buy tens of millions' worth of goods manufactured in Montreal, Toronto and other eastern industrial centres and we have the duty passed on to us; whatever charges are met, whether it be duty or sales tax or anything else, is passed on to the consumer in that province. So that there is no hon. gentleman so unsophisticated as to accept the figures which my hon. friend gave us last night in the sense in which he intended them to be taken. Let me take the position of Saskatchewan alone. It will be noted that the figures show this province contributing to the national revenue very much less per head than Manitoba. But Manitoba has the city of Winnipeg, which manufactures a considerable amount of goods and is a wholesale distributing point; almost all of our goods are received through Winnipeg. Naturally Winnipeg pays the taxes directly and passes them on to us. So I think we can very well dispose of that.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
May I interrupt the hon.
gentleman? The disconcerting feature is that the people of the western provinces do not seem to take kindly to buying Canadian goods. They want the duty taken off so that they can buy imported goods. That is what is worrying us. The west want the Hudson Bay railway completed so they may import goods direct from the Old Country. Unless they buy goods produced in Canada they are not contributing their per capita toward the
Railway Freight Rates

upkeep of the country. If they buy Canadian goods, then the case is different.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman's interruption is not relevant to the point in discussion. The protective tariff today compels us to buy home-manufactured goods whether we like it or not.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
You are opposing the
protective tariff.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
That is not under discussion at the present time. The fact is we do pay those taxes when we buy home-manufactured goods which to-day we are compelled to buy. Throughout almost the entire history of western Canada the people of those provinces have been compelled to pay from 25 to 40, 50 and even 100 per cent more on their freight rates than the people of eastern Canada. That is admitted. If we could have an actual equalization of the freight rate structure, we would have no objection whatsoever to the abrogation of the Crowsnest pass rates. I want to make that plain to hon. gentlemen. Just let the government lay down a policy of equalization of rates, and I think that not an hon. member in this section of the House will object to the complete abrogation of the Crowsnest pass agreement. The only reason why we are protesting against its partial abrogation is because we know there will be a distinct discrimination against us in any rates that are set by the Board of Railway Commissioners. Let us take the western rates case, which was heard before the railway commission in 1913, and judgment given the same year. In their judgment the Board of Railway Commissioners admitted frankly that there was serious discrimination against western Canada in the freight rate structure, but they justified that discrimination on the ground that the railways must carry goods cheaper in eastern Canada in order to meet water competition. That I may say is the reason, and the only reason, why we in the west are demanding the retention of some statutory protection against the discrimination that we know the Board of Railway Commissioners would inflict on us if they have a free hand. It is possible that Ontario and Quebec and the Maritime provinces may get a square deal, it is possible that the freight rate structure may be equalized in so far as those five provinces are concerned; but we in the prairie provinces know, as do hon. gentlemen from British Columbia-although they may not be quite ready to admit it-that the Board of Railway Commissioners will not give that province or the three prairie provinces a square deal and

make any attempt whatsoever to equalize freight rates as between eastern and western Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Why should my
hon. friend state "We know the railway commission will not give the prairie provinces a square deal"? That is not a fair statement to make.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Surely, Mr. Chairman,
we can judge what the Board of Railway Commissioners are likely to do by their actions in the past. We have their decision laid down in the western rates case, in which they admitted discrimination and justified it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
At that time the
whole field was covered with restrictions that prevented action on the part of the railway commission. The object of this legislation is to remove those restrictions and give the board an opportunity to equalize the rates.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
I would point out to
the Minister of Public Works (Mr. King, Kootenay) what I have already pointed out, that in the Speech from the Throne the government intimated the policy would be the equalization of freight rates. That would be perfectly satisfactory, but this bill does not provide for such equalization.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
That is the purpose of
the bill.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will
read the bill he will find it does not provide for equalization. Let me refer him to this one clause:
Notwithstanding the provisions of section three, the powers given to the board under this act to fix, determine and enforce just and reasonable rates, and to change and alter rates as changing conditions or cost of transportation may from time to time require,
and so on. That means we will have the rates worked out on the same old basis -as before.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: I know my hon. friend wants to be fair. Let me point out to him that the only restriction on the action of the board is that portion of the Crowsnest pass agreement which is retained. Does he wish that removed?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
I would be quite satisfied to see every vestige of the Crowsnest pass agreement removed if I knew that in the freight rate structure to be built up the railway commission would equalize freight rates as between provinces-the very thing that Was intimated in the Speech from the Throne. If that were done, I think every member in this section of the House would be prepared to see the complete abrogation of the Crowsnest pass agreement.

Railiuay Freight Rates

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: If my hon. friend will look at the order in council, he will find everything contained in it that he is complaining about.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: But the provisions of the order in council are not carried out in the bill. I am not a lawyer-

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: You ought to offer thanks for that.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: -but I fail to observe any particular instructions in this bill to the Board of Railway Commissioners to equalize freight rates as between provinces. That is the whole thing so far as we are concerned.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: The abject of this bill is to remove restrictions so that the Board of Railway Commissioners can carry out the terms of the order in council.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
There were very few restrictions on the board in 1913; why did they not do it then? The Crowsnest pass rates were not effective at that time because our grain and these other commodities were carried at rates less than those specified by the Crowsnest pass agreement. The railway commission was not hampered in their work in the least degree in 1913, and yet they admitted the discrimination, and they justified it and perpetuated it.
Now, the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) interjected a remark while the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. McMurray) was speaking, designed to show that there was a large deficit on the operation of the Canadian National Railways in western Canada. I would remind him that the railway commission have laid down the principle that in figuring rates the Canadian Pacific and not the Canadian National must be taken as the basis. I think every fair-minded member of this House and every fair-minded business man will admit that that is only right and proper. All the political crimes and blunders since confederation are welded together in the Canadian National Railways. Why, we have two thousand miles of duplication on the prairies, two thousand miles of railway that never should have been built. That was not the fault of the people of western Canada. That duplication is always going to involve a loss. We have three transcontinental railways that never were necessary, and a great deal of that unnecessary duplication has been shouldered on to western Canada. But in regard to the figures quoted by the hon. member for South Oxford, I would point out that in what is known as the western section, which covers everything from the head of the lakes-including I believe part of
the Transcontinental-to British Columbia, if we study the figures for the Canadian Northern railway previous to its being taken over by the government, and the corresponding figures for the Canadian Pacific Railway, we shall find that their operating ratio has always been a little higher in British Columbia than in the prairie provinces. That is, they had to spend more to earn a dollar in British Columbia. The prairie lines of the Canadian Pacific Railway have always been the most cheaply operated of the whole system; their operating ratio has always been lower than that for the other parts of the system. Now, after 1917 the Canadian Pacific Railway did not keep separate figures for the prairie lines, but included those and the British Columbia lines in the same statement. Therefore any figures that may be quoted either in regard to the Canadian National or the Canadian Pacific Railway in that regard are not fair to the prairies because they have to shoulder the very considerable loss or lower profit that should be chargeable to British Columbia.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: There must be a great deal of freight that originates at Fort William. Fort William is on the boundary line between the eastern and western sections. Is freight originating at Fort William credited to the eastern or the western section?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: I take it that any freight transported by rail from Fort William would be credited to the western section.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: I might tell the hon. member that Fort William is in the western section, and gets the credit.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
The officers representing the managements of both roads have pointed out that it is almost impossible ito properly separate the earnings of the different sections, so these Should not perhaps be taken as arbitrary.
I would like to quote a few figures in regard to the Canadian Pacific-I Shall not burden the House with very many. We find that from 1907 to 1911 inclusive, a period of five years, the Canadian Pacific railway produced net earnings, in the eastern section, of 843,500,000, and in the same period had net earnings over all expenses in western Canada of $91,500,000, a very much larger amount; from 1912 to 1916 inclusive, another five-year period, the eastern section produced net earnings of $60,000,000, and the western section, $152,000,000; from 1916 to 1920 inclusive, the eastern section produced $70,000,000, and the western section $144,000,000 of net earnings.
Now let us take the figures that really dhow what the earnings of the railways are, and
Railway Freight Rates

that is the operating ratio, or the amount that it is necessary to spend to earn a dollar. I am not going to quote extensively, butt in going over these figures I find that right from the beginning of the Canadian Pacific Railway's history the operating ratio on the prairies has been very much lower than it has been in eastern Canada, and I think there is no ground whatever for the contention that the operating costs in western Canada justify higher freight rates. When the contention is made that if the reductions that would be brought about if the Crowsnest rates were allowed to stand-and in this connection the Minister of Railways has pointed out that if those rates were permitted .to stand, the discrimination oomplaiined of to-day would have to be removed by the railways themselves, and I was very glad to hear him make that statement; he gave it as a reason Why the government should set aside .the agreement, but that is all -the more reason why we in the west want to see the agreement retained, because we never had any doubts in regard to that-if the Crowsnest rates were permitted to go into effect, I maintain that our railways are operated to-day, so far as their passenger service is concerned, in a way that no business' man, no manufacturer, no commercial institution in this country would tolerate. The railways are losing millions, and tens of millions, of dollars on their passenger service, and that loss on the passenger service has all to be shouldered by the freight service.
Now, what is the proper thing for us to do? To permit them to Charge rates high enough to allow them t'o continue, and go on losing millions of dollars on the passenger service, or force them to put the passenger service on a paying basis, or as near to that as
5 p.m. possible? I say they should be forced to -put the passenger service on a paying basis or as near as possible, and in 'that way pass the saving on t'o the freight Service.
Now let us take the Canadian National railway. In the year 1922 the freight earnings alone of the Canadian National Showed a surplus of $20,000,000.
Mr. Mc'M ASTER: Over operating expenses?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Yes. But the Canadian National in that same year had an operating deficit of $8,500,000 in its passenger service, and therefore, instead of turning in to the government that $20,000,000, or presenting a statement showing a surplus in the freight service of $20,000,000, the railway had to take out of that amount $8,500,000 to pay the deficit in its passenger service. In addition .to that, the value of the equipment used in the passen-

ger service is enormous. I have not the figures; I was not able to get them from the department.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: That is not taken into account in the operating expenses.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: I have given simply the operating figures, not 'taking into consideration the overhead.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: The cost of the equipment would not be reflected in the figures as to operating costs. They are not considered in that.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: I quite understand that. But I am pointing out that in addition to the $8,500,000 loss in the passenger service in 1922, there is an enormous overhead, and great depreciation through wear and tear on the equipment. I say that we are entitled to have that loss in the passenger service done away with, and the benefit passed on to the freight service. It can be done, and should be done.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Is the hon. member of the
opinion that if that improvement were made in the passenger service, the railways could afford to give this full reduction in freight rates?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
That is precisely my
point. I maintain that the railways could afford to give this complete reduction if they tried to operate their passenger service on a paying basis. Is there any business man in Canada who would say that there is any justification, for instance, for eighteen passenger trains a day passing between Ottawa and Montreal? That is one of the most absurd things I have ever known.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: What would the hon. member suggest as a means to eliminate that competition?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
If I were dictator in
charge of the situation, I would cut off about sixteen of those trains.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: What would you do supposing the management of one of the roads refused to cut off their share of the trains? Would you try to compete with them? What would be your method of dealing with that situation?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
I would not worry
about the management refusing to cut off the trains. I would put into effect reductions in freight rates that would compel them to reduce their passenger service.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
A reduction in passenger
rates?

Railway Freight Rates

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
In freight rates. Then
they would be compelled to reduce their passenger service to meet the cut in freight rates.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Put more pressure on the
railways?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Yes, and the only way
in which you can bring pressure upon them and force them to do it, is to reduce the freight rates. The Canadian Pacific railway, this wonderful institution whose marvellous efficiency we so often hear boasted about, is also losing an enormous sum of money on its passenger service. That is not generally known, but it is so. It has operating losses every year on its passenger service, I believe, not taking into consideration its overhead, and the wear and tear on its equipment; but it is not greatly concerned how much it loses just so long as we in this parliament permit it to charge sufficiently high tolls on the freight traffic. So long as they can meet out of their freight earnings the deficit in their passenger service, they do not need to be concerned at all. There is only one way in which we can force them to reduce the passenger service to a businesslike basis, and that is to reduce the freight rates to a proper basis, and 1 maintain that that can be done without the railways suffering any loss of revenue.
A few weeks ago I made a trip to Montreal. I went down there purposely to study this situation. About midway between Ottawa and Montreal-I thought it would be fair to take a point about midway between the two cities -I checked up the train and found there were 38 passengers on it, and there was accommodation on that train for 450 people! I could have gone out between the cars and almost thrown a stone over to another train of the Canadian Pacific railway going the same way, competitinjg for the same business, travelling to the same city. It is one of the most absurd situations imaginable, and yet it exists all over the country. Take the service between Montreal and Toronto, or take the transcontinental service. I can leave Winnipeg by two different trains leaving within fifty minutes or about an hour of each other. There is no necessity for it. There is no reason why there should not be only one transcontinental train a day. The Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National could run a train on alternate days, the Canadian Pacific leaving one day and the Canadian National the next.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
What answer would my
hon. friend give, for taking away the service, 280
to those people who do not live at the extreme ends of the line? In other words, if you take off the Canadian Pacific train on Thursday no person can be accommodated on that day except the man that lives in Winnipeg. All the intermediate and local points would be overlooked and they are of more importance, to my mind, than city points or just as much. That is the difficulty.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
I would give them
precisely the same answer that the Minister of Railways is giving us to-day when we are asking for lower freight rates-it cannot be done. That is a service that is not going to pay as far as local lines are concerned. I would point out though that a gasoline car operated between here and Montreal would have carried all the passengers on the particular train on which I travelled from Montreal a few days ago; there is no necessity for operating a very expensive passenger train for that service at all.
There is one thing that has struck me very forcibly all through this debate, and that is the attitude of our friends in the east. One hon. member asked the other night why the Crows-nest pass rates should not be given to Quebec. Perhaps the hon. member in question was not aware that Quebec to-day has lower rates than the Crowsnest pass rates. But I want to point this out: it seems to be the fight of the prairie provinces, whether the freight moves east or moves west, regardless who has to pay for it. If we get any benefit in the matter of reduced rates on our products going out surely Ontario gets some benefit from its products moving to the prairie provinces. That angle of the question seems to be forgotten by hon. members from the eastern provinces. I want to point this out also: that just as soon as you raise the freight rates on flour, feed, and any of these other products coming east, you are going to raise your own cost of living; you are going to increase the price of bran, shorts, and flour to everyone desirous of using these commodities in eastern Canada. It is a problem for you gentlemen in the east just as much as it is a problem for us; and the solution of that problem would mean as much to you as it does to us. And let me say further in regard to the thirteen commodities on which the rates were reduced when moved west:	That reduction made a
market for your Ontario products in the western prairies which this legislation will do away with. Surely there can be no question as to that. And yet my hon. friends in Ontario do not seem to realize that it is to their interest as well as ours to maintain reduced rates on all these commodities moving

Railway Freight Rates

between the east and the west. These consist of apples, fresh fruits, furniture, building material, agricultural implements, fence wire, dairy cattle, and some other items.
Now what about the problem of British Columbia? The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) last night enunciated what I presume is the policy of the official opposition. He pointed out that the proper and logical thing to do was to leave the Board Of Railway Commissioners free and unhampered-absolutely free and unhindered by any statutory agreements or limitations-so as to give them a complete and free hand in the building up of a new freight scale. Looking at the question in an abstract way I would be inclined to agree with the hon. member, I would think that from an academic standpoint that would be a right and proper course to take; but there is a human side to this question which we cannot overlook, and while I do not feel like criticizing the personnel of the Board of Railway Commissioners, we know that in the past we have not had a square deal from the board. No one knows this better than my hon. friends from British Columbia. If there is any one province or any one part of the Dominion which is dependent upon another, it is British Columbia with regard to the prairie provinces. Those provinces are the principal market for the fruit, the lumber, the building material, and all the other products of British Columbia. But what has the freight schedule done for that market in the past? Why it has simply been used as a protective tariff; and I draw the attention of my hon. friend for Nanaimo (Mr. Dickie), who asked me a question a few moments ago, to the fact that the freight rates to-day operate as a protective tariff at the Rocky Mountains to prevent British Columbia products from entering the prairie provinces, and I believe that it has been deliberately designed with that end in view. Let me quote a few of these discriminatory freight rates. Taking the regular classification I find that from Vancouver to Kamloops, a distance of 250 miles, the first class rate is $1.34.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: On what?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
On any first class commodity. From Montreal to Wylie, a distance .of 253 miles, about the same mileage, the first class rate is 75J cents; and I can go all down the scale and show you instance after instance where it looks as if the whole freight rate schedule were intended to keep the manufactured products of British Columbia out of the prairie provinces and leave those [Provinces as a preserve for the eastern manufacturers. In other words it does the very 
thing on a limited scale that the protective tariff does in a national way. From Vancouver to Marquette, a distance of 1,437 miles, the first class freight rate is $3.99. From Montreal to Marquette, a distance of 1,446 miles, the first class rate is $2.76. What a discrimination against British Columbia! And yet my hon. friends from that province think that if they give the Board of Railway Commissioners a free and unfettered hand in this matter they would get a square deal. I have more respect for their intelligence than to think that they actually believe that.
Now let us take the rates on sugar. From Vancouver to Morse, Saskatchewan, a distance of 994 miles the rate is $1.41, but from Montreal to Fort William, 996 miles, or about the same mileage, the rate is only seventy-nine cents, just a little over one-half. Now sugar is one of the principal products of British Columbia, and the prairies are its logical market. (British Columbia is the source from which we should get most of our sugar, but with a freight rate of such a character we are compelled to get our sugar from the Montreal refiners whether we like it or not. So I say again that this freight schedule operates as a protective tariff, deliberately designed I believe, to keep the products of British Columbia out of the prairie provinces. I find also that from Vancouver to Brandon, a distance of 1,333 miles, the sugar rate is $1.60 a hundred. From Montreal to Rennie, Manitoba, a distance of 1,343 miles, about the same mileage, the rate is $1.11, and so on down the scale. I have a great many figures here but I do not wish to worry the House by quoting them. The same thing is true of lumber. Of course British Columbia supplies most of the lumber to-day, but some of these freight rates were established at an earlier period when [DOT] lumber was being shipped from the east to the west.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Is British Columbia lumber shipped at a commodity rate?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: On a commodity rate, but a much higher rate is imposed on lumber shipped into the prairie provinces than on eastern lumber moved for the same distance.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: In Ontario the shipments are made on a commodity rate.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
I think that lumber is shipped on a commodity rate no matter where it is going, at least from mills of any particular size. Now let me take the case of rice. Vancouver imports rice from the Orient, and I believe that city is the logical

Railway Freight Rates
distributing point for the whole Dominion. Now, the rate on rice from Vancouver to Calgary is seventy-five cents a hundred; that from Vancouver to Montreal is also seventy-five cents a hundred. In other words that rice is carried by the railway companies from Calgary to Montreal, a distance of about 2,400 miles, absolutely free. For the benefit of whom? For the benefit of the Montreal distributor.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: The Vancouver distributor.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Not Vancouver, but
Montreal.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Not at all.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: I want to point out to the minister that the Montreal distributor gets his rice from Vancouver at seventy-five cents a hundred. The distributor at Vancouver should be able to supply the local demands of the prairies. That is the logical place from which to supply those demands. I think there should be no difference of opinion on that point.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: I was not arguing on that at all. The commodity rates are for this purpose alone; to aid the industry at the point where the commodity is shipped. The commodity rate given to Vancouver, as my hon. friend says, is a very low one, in order that Vancouver might put rice into Montreal. That is the object.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
I contend that in this
case the rate is given, not to Vancouver at all, but to Montreal, because it does not go through the Vancouver distributor. The Montreal importer can import it direct from the Orient and possibly, deliver it back on the prairies and take the market from the Vancouver distributor.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: It is absurd.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Certainly it is absurd.
It means that the railway companies are receiving an exorbitant rate that is almost confiscation for carrying the rice from Vancouver to Calgary, or else they are carrying it at a distinct loss from Calgary to Montreal; either one of those two conditions obtain. There can be no question about it, and just as long as you permit the railways to carry anything at a loss, you must burden something else with the loss, and that is one reason we have high rates and why those rates are being maintained. If there is one part of Canada dependent upon another, it is British Columbia which is dependent on the prairie provinces. As we prosper in the prairies,
British Columbia will prosper. As our farmers get into a position to buy your fruit, your lumber, your sugar and all the other products that you are producing, in British Columbia to-day, you will prosper, and you will prosper only in so far as we prosper. There is no mistake about that, and yet I say that in the four years that I have been in this House, on almost every issue that means anything to the prairie provinces, I see the British Columbia members lined up almost to a man against us. Yet I say that the interests of British Columbia are tied up directly with the interests of the prairie provinces.
I have a great deal of sympathy with the Minister of Railways, and I think Canada is fortunate indeed to have a man like the present Minister of Railways in charge of that department. When I hear expressions of opinion of hon. members behind the minister and realize what some hon. gentlemen in his party would do with this great enterprise, then I thank heaven we have such a man at the head of that department. I wish again to make one last appeal to the government to igo into the question of passenger service very .thoroughly. I find after discussing this matter with business men and newspaper men in Montreal that they see the absurdity of the position; they do not want eighteen trains a day passing between Montreal and Ottawa. It is only a matter of getting together and holding a club over the heads of the railways, and that club would be the reduction of freight rates. If the minister would say to the railways, "You must reduce your freight rates, or show very good reasons why you should be dipping into the receipts from freight in order to bolster up the passenger service that is not paying," it might have a good result. The onus is on the railways to do that. I think the transcontinental passenger service can be cut down, and the use of a few gasoline cars here and there will give just as good service as the people are getting to-day.

What do we know about it? What point have we in common after yesterday's discussion and to-day's discussion? What real practical thought have we got about the underlying principles on which freight rates have to be made? We have to do two things, first, to see that our railways can function and continue to function, and, secondly, that in functioning our rates shall be so arranged as to give each and every part of the country opportunity itself to function having again particular regard to the main activities of each part of the country. The solution of the freight rate burden of this country is not to be found in paper freight rates at all. I do not know whether that is a good thing or not. It might

be worse. But let us get back to the genesis of railway rates. They should be rates which, in the first instance, would render it possible for the country's business to move surely and profitably and, in the second instance, rates which would enable the companies to continue to live. Let me take some of the illustrations which were given by an hon. gentleman who gave us one or two illustrations as to freight rates. You may have a high rate in one section of the country in connection with, traffic that it is not very greatly interested in and a low rate in connection with traffic that it is interested in, and you imay have a condition where, instead of having one low rate, you have many; or, on the other hand you may have a condition where, instead of having one high rate, you have many, and you may find that traffic is carried in the district in which there are many high rates cheaper than it is in some district with many low rates.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Is that justifiable? I am asking purely for information.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
It entirely
depends. What must be kept in view is the desire to enable business to be carried on properly. There ought to be put into force such rates as will enable districts to function and give a first consideration to the primary activities of each district, making that the chief object. If you do that, carrying it right down, you get to the point where of necessity you must charge higher rates on some things to the very great advantage of the district.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: I am inclined to agree wiih my hon. friend; I think there is a great deal in his argument. But I would point out that it does not square with the theory of equalizing freight rates. I think the idea of absolutely equalizing freight rates is a hazy dream.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
My hon. friend is largely right. When .you talk about an equalization of freight rates you are faced with an ever-changing proposition, for one thing. The demands of business are not the same everywhere; they are not constant. What is necessary to move certain traffic here to-day may be necessary over there tomorrow. We may go wrong in one of two ways. In the first place, it is wrong to have equality in relation to unequal things, and it is just as wrong to have unequal treatment in dealing with equal things. The one is just as wrong and vicious as the other, and the fact is so obvious that it needs only to be

stated in order to be appreciated. After all what is it that the people are interested in? They are not interested in the theoretical amount chargeable in a great long list of freight rates; what they are interested in is the actual cost of moving actual traffic. And all freight rates are reducible to one common factor everywhere, namely, the return to the company per ton mile. How much is the company getting out of it? That is the question. The amount collected from the public is the real thing in which the people are interested.
Mr. McMASTER Suppose there is a district producing a valuable mineral ore as well as a considerable quantity of wheat; would it be fair to carry the wheat out of that district at a- charge below cost of carriage because, from the same district, a high enough rate could be imposed on the mineral ore to make the carriage on the whole profitable?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: I can answer that frankly. In connection with all freight rates we must consider these three points: first, the question of public necessity; second, the cost of service; and, third, the amount of added value of the property to the owner by reason of transportation. My hon. friend deals now with a valuable ore. Well, that is worth nothing without transportation, whereas, transportation being provided, it is of great value to the owner. In connection with any commodity in relation to which the percentage of cost of transportation to the total value secured in the ultimate market is insignificant, I would say that the railway should charge enough to make it possible to carry that freight covering all possible charges with a profit. On a valuable ore, I should think that the freight ought to be relatively high.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Does not that mean in effect that the railway board should regulate freight rates in such a way as practically to tax one man's business in order to make another man's profitable? Is that just?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: But the whole shop belongs to one man or one company.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Perfectly true;
the illustration I readily admit is not a very good one. One really needs a blackboard to

illustrate these questions properly; but suppose we assume that this sheet of paper which I hold in my hand is a 'blackboard. Suppose we have at the top of the board "100 per cent", representing the sum of money which will enable the railway company to function properly, to pay its costs of maintenance and betterments, its taxes, its interest on bonds, and its overhead charges and fair profit. All that is represented by 100 per cent. We will assume that a line midway down this hypothetical blackboard, marked "50 per cent", represents the actual cost of operation entirely apart from all overhead charges, the cost of operation involved in the actual movement of traffic. Let us assume further that there are fifty people living in the district who by their efforts are producing enough to meet that 100 per cent; and there are five more who come in, newcomers,who want to go into the business of growing wheat. Now, they cannot pay any high freight rate on that commodity and it is perfectly obvious that if their rate be below the 50 per cent line they are penalizing the people that are already there. But if instead of taking a rate below the 50 per cent line, we take from the wheat grower enough to give us 60, assuming that the proportion of tonnage of wheat is equal, it is clear that 10 per cent being added to the upper register, as it were, the general burden on the fifty people who were there first falls from 100 to 90. And that is exactly the situation which my hon. friend puts in regard to the ore and the wheat.

speechtext: I am afraid I have not been able to follow entirely the illustration given by my hon. friend. subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: No. The genesis of all freight rates was the old common law yard stick of what the services were worth; and that old yard stick was something that always related to the value of the commodity carried. There were two reasons for it: the value of the service was greater to the owner of the commodity as the value of his commodity increased the more, and the carrier's risk was infinitely greater.

iSir HENRY DRAYTON: Well, Mr. Chairman, every country in the world recognizes the principle that I have been talking about, whether they have rate-regulating commissions or not. That is the reason we have ten classes of freight and commodity rates without end. If these concessions were not made by the railways in ease of business, we would not have business moving in essential lines; that is simply all there is to it. speechtext: Mr. Chairman, when we arose at six o'clock I had been dealing with the railway rates per ton per mile, and I had also referred to the argument made by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) in connection with the tariffs. Now, I want to say, in fairness to that hon. gentleman, that his argument is just as true, just as cogent and just as reasonable as any argument advanced by the late Solicitor General (Mr. McMurray). I am not going to take up the time of the House in going over those arguments, which were based not upon exact figures or facts, but I am going to take the concrete case given by the hon. member for Mackenzie in connection with the rate of seventy-five cents on rice, which rate he said was hurting Vancouver and enabling Montreal to get this commodity in cheaply and distribute it in quantities in territories where Vancouver ought to have the right of distribution. I say in fairness to him that he is absolutely honest in what he says but absolutely mistaken and absolutely wrong. But he is no more mistaken and no more wrong than-

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Did he not say Calgary?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Oh no, Vancouver. The rate of seventy-five cents from Vancouver to Montreal-

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
-and the same rate to Calgary. I have taken the trouble to look up the records. This is a case I happen to know something about. In the first instance rice only came into Canada from two sources. Originally it came from the Orient altogether, and the distributing points for the Canadian rice markets were Vancouver in the west, on the one hand, and New Orleans in the south on the other hand. Vancouver desired to be able to go into the rice business in competition with New Orleans. But New Orleans is much nearer the eastern territory than Vancouver. The Canadian Pacific put that rate in. It put in a specially low commodity rate to enable Vancouver to distribute rice to Canadian territory in competition with New Orleans. No one could quarrel with that motive. It was a good thing for Vancouver, it was also a good thing for the country. It gave the country the possibility of having competition in rice, instead of leaving the whole of the eastern part of Canada entirely at the mercy of the distributors in New Orleans. I do not think that any hon. gentleman would seriously complain of that. Now then, how does it work out? The hon. member for Mackenzie says that is something which hurts Vancouver and is there to help Montreal. Well now, it is extraordinary that the Montreal people-

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Is not my hon. friend wrong in stating that the hon. member for Mackenzie says it hurts Vancouver? I do not recall that statement at all.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
No, he said it hurt Vancouver by enabling rice to be put cheaply into Montreal, and enabling Montreal to send that rice back into territory it otherwise could not reach. There is no question as to what was said. But the Montreal people did not take that view. Montreal got started in the rice business, and desired to get a rate so as to be able to distribute rice upon a proportionate basis, and the Mount Royal Milling and Manufacturing Company, which is the Montreal company, after complaining about this rate for years, made formal application to the Board of Railway Commissioners They complained as to this special commodity blanket rate of seventy-five cents per hundred pounds, applicable as it is on cleaned rice in car load lots, from Vancouver to practically all points of importance in the prairie provinces and Ontario and Quebec, that it was effective right through the whole of their own local territory, and they asked that the discrimination be removed. And what was the discrimination? Their rate from Montreal to Vancouver was $2.42 as against a rate from Vancouver to Montreal of seventy-five cents. Their rate from Montreal to Calgary was $2, as against a rate from Vancouver to Calgary of seventy-five cents. Their rate to Edmonton was also $2, as against the blanket rate of seventy-five cents. Their rate to Regina was $1.55 as against the seventy-five cent rate, the rate to Saskatoon $1.68; the rate to Brandon $1.23, and the rate to Winnipeg $1.14 from Montreal, as against seventy-five cents from Vancouver. Well, as I say, the hon. gentleman's argument that this rate was a hardship to Vancouver is no worse than other arguments we have heard in connection with this rate situation.
I am not going to waste any more time chasing phantoms in connection with the different points raised in argument by hon. members in regard to this freight business, but I am going back to the question which is the real governing question, which shows just exactly how much money is taken out of a district by a railway, namely the rate per ton per mile. I submit, Mr. Chairman, what I know to be the fact, and it is a result that I am frank to say I take a great deal of pride in; that the work of equalization, not that

equalization which aims at making unequal things equal, which is an impossibility, not insuring equal treatment to unequal, thingg, and thereby bringing about direct discrimination in fact, although not on paper; but an equalization which fixes the whole run of the traffic in such a way as to bring about practically the same result in this field of immense diversity and diversion. It is a tremendous task to perform. It is a task that takes years, and I do not for one minute say that it ever can be actually accomplished. Make your loadings and make your rates on the business of this year or that year, and you will be wrong, because with the very best intentions, following the matter up just as closely as it is humanly possible to do, hon. members will find that the percentages of this loading and that loading change from time to time, and inevitably you get differences in your results. You must get them indeed, unless we are going to treat grain just exactly the same way as you treat gold or anything else. But there the happy chance lies. Let us put it that way, that the happy chance made it in that year 1917 so that there was such absolute equality, not in rate tables, which mean nothing, but in the actual amount of money taken out of the people in the different parts of the country per ton per mile, that there is a difference only of one hundredth part of a cent, and I say it is the closest result, so far as I know, that has ever been obtained.
Rates are delicate things and they can do a great deal towards making or breaking the country. I am going to illustrate what I mean by that. Hon. members will pardon me if I have to refer to myself, because I am speaking of my own knowledge, my own action and judgment, but when I went on the railway board in 1912 there was no Drumheller coal in Winnipeg. The American coal had1 the market. It was actually carried as far west as Saskatoon. As a result of no hit-or-miss jumping at conclusions but as a result of a long, tedious investigation into the question of coal rates, including cost and the 'like, in the judgment of 1914 the whole basis was changed, and in consequence of that change it was but a short time before not only was there no American coal in Saskatoon, Regina, Moose Jaw and other like places, but the Canadian coal was absolutely controlling the markets there and selling largely in Winnipeg. You cannot get these results by acts of parliament. You can only get them by honest, long, painstaking efforts and endeavour. After 1917 we had different increases. You cannot preserve a proper equality of return when you are in the business of percentage increase. The need

tariffs, but simply to the change in the traffic. Another point that I want to make clear to my hon. friends is this, and it is a point which we all should know about. If you have a low operating ratio, traffic which moves in great volume even at a low fixed rate may be very remunerative. Hon. members must realize that at one time, in my opinion, the grain traffic was the most remunerative traffic in this country. That, I know, is a conclusion that many railway men do not agree with, but I do not agree with them.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: In what years would that be?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Before costs went up when we had a low operating ratio. Before the rate increases came up, we had in western Canada, a splendid operating ratio, one of the best operating ratios in the world. If you have a low operating ratio, so long as you are always below your low rate, and you have great density of traffic, you have great profits. We had tremendous density of traffic in the grain business. I have been making a little calculation based on a theoretical rate in order to give hon. members some idea of what I mean. For example, supposing you take a low rate structure; supposing you take an average ton-mile rate- and this is not out of the way as compared with what we used to have-of 55, and supposing you have a grain rate such as we have now of .52, that does not appear to be a tremendous difference; but if you were going to move seven billion ton miles if sixty per cent, of that business was grain and you made a fair distribution of costs and if you had an operating ratio as high as 70-and the Canadian Pacific used to have in western territory an operating ratio as low as 62-you would have an operating profit of $5,400,000 on this grain traffic even at that low rate. You have your tremendous density and a movement which of itself is comparatively cheap. There is practically no yardage in connection with grain. The railway company is as a rule, at no expense either to load or unload the cars, and although the rate looks small, there was good money in it. Hon. gentlemen, however, must realize that when you are dealing with a business tremendous in its volume, where profits are made in the decimals of cents that I gave to the committee, if that decimal is wrong only a little way, the losses are correspondingly great. One thing that makes ansmne who really wants to see business properly carried on in this country feel sad and depressed is the way in which hon. gentlemen here will not look facts in the face and will make statements which,
Railway Freight Rates

although they may believe in them, are absolutely misleading and which they have only to turn to their own records to know are absolutely misleading. A difference of a few decimal points has worked a tremendous change in our railway situation. While before the grain business was profitable, today it is not.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Why is it that in the grain moving season the monthly net profits jump so tremendously?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: My hon. friend will find, as regards the months when the net profits rise, there is really no such thing as a monthly net profit. There are approximations which are put in from time to time, but you do not know what your profits are until the end of the accounting year. He will also find in connection with those self same months there is a movement of high class freight. I am not going into speculation; I want to give the facts, but I want the committee to understand first the reasons for those facts. I want hon. gentlemen to understand this: I have taken the position always consistently that I believe these grain rates and flour rates should be very low. I believe in looking after them; I believe in seeing that the west can properly function; but I believe in everybody knowing what we are doing. I believe in the truth, in looking the truth in the face, and in justifying a rate which will enable the west properly to function. I do not believe we shall ever get a unified country if hon. gentlemen from the west persist in making the claim that they are supporting the railways of Canada. I was pointing out that the difference of a very few decimal points makes a tremendous difference in connection with the results. I have supporting statements for that view.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Do I understand my hon. friend is arguing that the present grain rates are not profitable to the railways?

speechtext: I do not think anyone will suggest that the Great Northern was very short-sighted in its pblicy, and I am sure their judgment would suggest still higher rates. Be that as it may, that is the situation.

speechtext:
Did the
Great Northern get any such assistance as was given the Canadian Pacific Railway?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
I do not think it did. There were railways on the American side that did receive great assistance but I do not think the Great Northern did. The earlier American roads got land grants but this policy was soon stopped, and rightly so. But let us remember that every single cent of the Great Northern is shown there, while in connection with the Canadian Pacific, which is supposed to earn seven per cent on its investment in railways, so much of the favours which they got has been converted into property against which there is no charge that the earnings amount only to about 4.4 or 4.3.
I want to give to the committee the exact results of calculations made not by myself but by the statistical bureau of the Canadian National Railways. In these analyses no reference whatever is made to the operations of the Duluth, Winnipeg and Pacific railway, so that the results are as far as possible free from any American rate influence. The grain operating ratio for 1923 was 126.14 per cent, resulting in an operating loss of $6,088,499. In 1924 the grain operating ratio was 126.96, the operating loss being $5,812,016. Freight traffic other than grain produced on the other hand in 1923 net earnings amounting to $8,276,195 and in 1924, $10,432,831. Anyone
who will take the trouble to go over the figures will be convinced that the statements that are made to the effect that the west is carrying the east are untrue. In 1923, in the western territory, excluding the Duluth, Winnipeg and Pacific railway, the railway operating revenues amounted to $66,000,000 odd and the expenses to $70 000,000 odd, leaving a net deficit in that year of $2,105,741. Can there be any honest dispute about this, unless on the part of some excited person on the hustings? Analyse .these figures and you will get the revenue from passenger and allied services. Now, the hon. member (Mr. Campbell) was perfectly right when he said that passenger service does not pay. I have been saying the same thing day in and day out throughout this parliament when the question was up, and that is one of the reasons why we are absolutely insane in connection with our purchases of rolling stock. It is for instance absolutely ludicrous to buy $44,000,000 worth of rolling stock comprising in large part passenger locomotives and expensive coaches, and that in two years alone.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Is not the real reason
to be found in the fact that trains are run half empty?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman may try to palliate it as much as he likes, but the fact is that passenger business even in thickly populated centres does not pay, and the United States management regard the thickly populated peopled suburban areas near large centres as the only places where they can make money out of the passenger traffic. There is no mystery about it; every railway man knows that this is the case. And my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) is also partly right. We can reduce the loss in part by running fewer trains and by putting a stop to the expenditure of some $1,200,000 for the purpose of advertising passenger trains. We could get rid of some of that loss if we stopped radio and a few more frills. But still there would be a loss. Each year there has been a substantial deficit on passenger business. Bringing in all these things, we have that deficit as I have stated. In 1924 we had a deficit of $1,240,353 on these lines. Now, hon. gentlemen to my left-so far the ex-Solicitor General (Mr. McMurray) is the only supporter of the government who has joined them-were well represented on the committee that investigated the Canadian National Railway accounts, and every member of the Progressive party on that committee has gone through those accounts, but I have never heard any sug-
Railway Freight Rates

gestion from them that the accounts were falsified; if they were, it was their business to show it. The hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Stewart) has put in a lot of work on these accounts, and he understands them. He has found nothing wrong with them. If we want to be honest with ourselves, we will stop this idle talk that the west is carrying the east, when everyone knows that the fact is absolutely the opposite. We have had large earnings in eastern Canada, as against losses in western Canada and in the Mari times.
Now, some hon. gentlemen say, "You cannot raise rates in eastern Canada on account of water competition." I just wonder how many of those who indulge in that talk really think there is anything in it except so much nonsense. Has not the cost of water operation gone up? Does not everybody know it? Cannot raise the rates in eastern Canada! Why, the rates on pretty nearly every bit of farm produce grown in eastern Canada were raised from 80 to 83 per cent, and they are still up. Hon. gentlemen from farm constituencies in Ontario and Quebec know the state of their rate situation. The ex-Solicitor General actually says, "You cannot raise rates at all in central Canada because of water competition." Well, I should like him for once to look at a tariff, to take a real interest in this situation, and to go and tell the farmers of Ontario and Quebec that their rates cannot be raised because of water competition. The truth is that the rates of the farmers of central Canada on butter, cheese, eggs-the very things that they are interested in-were raised as high as S3 per cent, and only a thin shaving has been taken off. They are still at that high level, and we might as well tell the truth about it.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
The bill before the House has been under discussion since yesterday, and in introducing it the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) outlined the extent to which it will go. It is proposed by this legislation that the restrictions imposed under the Crowsnest pass agreement of 1897 shall be entirely eliminated, except in the case of grain and flour moving east to Fort William in the territory that was previously considered Crowsnest pass territory. My hon. friend, the member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton), who has had great experience and possesses a great knowledge of this matter by reason of his having been formerly chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners of Canada, has just indicated to the House that the government have probably not gone as far as they should, but still has suggested that it is good business that special consideration should be given to the rates on grain and flour, commodities produced in the western provinces. In fact he has gone further and said that this would be the practice of the railway board and the railways themselves, and I think in that respect he is correct. I think it has been the policy of the railway commission and the railway companies to give special consideration to these commodities which have so much to do with the prosperity of our friends in western Canada and the prosperity of the province of British Columbia. Now, this matter is one of national importance and it is before this House which represents, or should represent national ideas. It is here that, we should settle what is best in the interests of Canada, and not what is best in the interests merely of one particular section or the other. We should review the whole situation-and the railway situation is a very large and important one-and endeavour to come to a right decision from a national standpoint. We should decide what is best to do for the Canadian people as a whole, not what is best to do for the people of Alberta, or Saskatchewan, or British Columbia, or the Maritimes. Have the government presented a fair proposition in connection with this matter? I think they have. I think it is generally conceded that the Crowsnest agreement entered into in 1897 could not in fair-281
ness to the railways or to other parts of the country, be continued in full effect. That must be conceded by all hon. members. As my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) said yesterday, the economic conditions resulting from the war preclude such a course. Therefore at this time it is necessary for us to consider what is best to be done in the interests of Canada.
There are some who say that we should wipe out all restrictions and leave the whole matter to be dealt with by the Board of Railway Commissioners. That would have been a fairly comfortable and easy way out of the situation for the government, and I have little doubt if they had brought down such a policy it would have received the endorsement of the House. However, the government has considered that in the great interior of Canada we have problems that are of interest to the eastern and western portions of the Dominion as well as to the territory directly affected. Consequently special rates have been retained on grain and flour which will be the maximum within the Crowsnest pass territory. The Minister of Railways, when explaining the bill yesterday, said that of necessity these rates should be made applicable not only to lines that were constructed in 1897 but to all lines that are in existence in that area. If the problem is there and has to be met there should be such an extension. We people in British Columbia have some knowledge of the Crowsnest pass agreement. We were told yesterday that the parliament of Canada had voted a subsidy of some $3,000,000 odd for the construction of this road, but that in lieu of that subsidy the Canadian Pacific Railway Company had secured this agreement. But it should not be forgotten that the province of British Columbia was the largest contributor to the construction of this railway. The road was built under what was known as the British Columbia Southern charter, a provincial charter, which gave a very large land grant within the province of British Columbia to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to construct the road. The $3,000,000 that was voted by parliament, a subsidy at the rate of $11,000 a mile was not the primary consideration. However, we in British Columbia have derived benefits from the construction of the line. It opened up a very rich portion of that province, an area rich in timber, minerals, coal and other resources, and the development of that territory brought prosperity to our province. In fact the construction of the line induced a period of great growth and activity in the

Kootenay country, and did much to recoup the treasury of the province for the obligations which it had undertaken. We have undoubtedly received benefits from that railway construction but it should not be lost sight of that British Columbia was a large contributor in the first place. When the Crowsnest pass agreement was entered into British Columbia was not an exporting province; it was pretty much self contained. It was only after the construction of this railway, that the northwestern provinces and British Columbia felt the life blood stirring in their veins and began to grow and become important provinces in this Dominion. Whether or not the policy of the government of that day was the stimulant that brought about the large immigration into and settlement of the northwest, I am not prepared to say, but I think we can fairly claim that it was a very important contributing factor. Certainly in British Columbia we have enjoyed, to some extent, that settlement and development. Such being the case we are deeply interested in the further development of the central portion of Canada. Personally, from my own experience and knowledge, I believe that we are more deeply interested even than we were in those early days. The opportunities are there, and it should be the policy of this government or of governments that may follow to try and bring about a proper settlement of that great interior portion of Canada. My hon. friend from Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) made a rather startling statement when he said that there was a group over there who were prepared to cut out entirely any concession given by the Crowsnest pass agreement. If that is so, I wonder if my hon. friend really represents the true thought of that great interior west. If that is true, and if that is the real thought of the interior west, then this problem could be solved very easily as far as this government is concerned.

speechtext:

Discrimination so authorized by parliament itself cannot be regarded as unjust or prohibited.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: You can get rates without alleging discrimination.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: But that ground is removed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
My hon. friend
advanced the same point yesterday and it was fully met by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald, Pictou). This legislation does not limit the power of the board in dealing with grain and flour rates, but having fixed a maximum rate it will have a controlling effect generally. That is the only effect it will have. I should think that the parliament of Canada if it adopted this legislation would have indicated to the Board of Railway Commissioners that in its opinion it was in the interests of the people that grain and grain products should have the advantage of the cheapest possible transportation in order that these commodities might be moved to the seaports of Canada for export. That is what is indicated in this legislation and I should think it would be a guiding principle to the commission.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Can the minister justify this legislation in relation to grain and flour going westward?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Let me read far the benefit of the hon. gentleman the following paragraph from the order in council:
The committee are further of the opinion that as the production and export of grain and flour forms one of the chief assets of the Dominion, and in order to encourage the further development of the great graingrowing provinces of the west, on which development the future of Canada in large measure depends, it is desirable that the maximum cost of the transportation of these products should be determined and known, and therefore are of opinion that the maximum established for rates on grain and flour, as at present in force under the Crowsnesrt; pass agreement, should not be exceeded.
That is a fair declaration of policy, and it is I think important, in the interests of the country, that the movement of these products to the sea board should be facilitated at the lowest possible cost.

'Mr. McQUARRIE:	From the standpoint
of British Columbia, how could the fixing of a maximum rate westward for grain and flour injure that province?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: It might not injure British Columbia, but parliament having declared that this should extend into British Columbia it would have a limiting effect on the Board of Railway Commissioners in dealing with traffic which we hope will flow from British Columbia into the prairie provinces. The people of British Columbia, as I have said, are anxious to see the western grain movement facilitated; but we are more anxious to see the elimination of what is known as the mountain scale. I am satisfied that with this legislation, and with the scope of reference to the railway commission cleared up, we may look forward to the day when British Columbia will not be discriminated against as she has been in the past. My hon. friend speaks of the railway commission. Well, he must also remember that there is an appeal from that body. The direction of the government in the order in council is explicit on the matter, and the legislation is also plain and direct. It deals with one phase only of the fixing of rates, and in other respects it removes all limitations that have heretofore been operating against British Columbia, preventing that province from obtaining what it considers its just due.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Does the minister say that it removes all the discriminations against which that province has been fighting?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: I say that it removes from the field the limitations that heretofore have existed and gives to the railway commission full scope to consider properly the claims of British Columbia.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: But it leaves a serious discrimination against the western movement of grain.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: There is no discrimination; it is left to the Board of Railway Commissioners to fix what they consider a proper and fair rate on grain moving westward.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Why not do the same with the grain moving eastward?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
For that matter,
why not fix a rate on coal moving either eastward or westward? I think our experience yesterday and to-day will show us how utterly absurd such an undertaking would be.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Why start it then?
