speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
I think we have
explained fairly why the government have taken this step. I have read the clause in the order in council showing clearly why we have considered this policy essential to the development not only of western Canada but of the Dominion as a whole. Now, my hon. friend from North Vancouver yesterday referred to the Vancouver Sun of June 6 and intimated that I had said so and so. Let me say in reply that I am no more responsible for what appears in the press than he is himself. I find in the same issue of the Sun that the hon. member is reported as expressing unqualified approval of the government policy. He is also reported as saying:
The recommendation to the railway commissioners to hold thorough investigation into traffic east and west via the Panama is sound. The whole freight rates structure should be revamped on distribution from both Atlantic and Pacific sea-board inward.
That is what the government has in view.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
The minister referred to the member for "North Vancouver." That happens to be in my constituency and I want to say that I gave no such interview as the minister attributes to me.
M.r. KING (Kootenay):	I meant the hon.
member for Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens). But I would refer the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clark) to his own statement. He said that Saskatchewan and Alberta would pay nearly double the rate under this legislation that they would pay to Buffalo and New York. My hon. friend was not serious when he made that statement. He knows where the dividing line is in Alberta; and under the adjustments that have taken place since 1922 one-fourth of the discrimination has been wiped out, and to-day there are points in Alberta that have a preference and will continue to have a preference to the ports of the Pacific. As the discriminations are removed that line will move further eastward. But my hon. friend could not successfully contend for one moment that wheat moving from Alberta or Saskatchewan to the Pacific coast would pay double the rate applicable to wheat moving to Buffalo or New York, although he made that statement yesterday.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Is it not a fact that the rate on wheat from Edmonton to Fort William is practically the same as from Edmonton to Vancouver?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: I think there is a difference of three to five cents per hundred pounds.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: One cent difference?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
No, more than
that.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
The difference is two
and a half cents'-22| against 25.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: There is a preference there anyway and we can come as far east as Medicine Hat at the present time. This question is not only of interest to British Columbia and to the prairie provinces, but to the whole of Canada, and I believe that under the policy laid down by the government an opportunity will be given the railway board to effect an equalization of freight rates by building up a new rate structure that will enure to the advantage of the whole Dominion.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have
no desire to prolong this debate, but L should like to say one or two things in reference to some of the statements made yesterday. Some hon. members seem to be under the impression that the government by this legislation is fixing freight rates. Nothing of the kind is taking place. The rates on grain and flour are fixed by the Crowsnest pass agreement-a contract that was entered into almost thirty years ago, a contract that was duly signed and delivered, the consideration for which was fully paid by the people of Canada. That contract was made by the parliament of Canada with the railway company, but parliament acted in a representative capacity, the real party in interest being the people of Canada. The people paid the money, the people acquired the rights-rights that were vested not in the parliament but in the people of Canada. That contract should be regarded as sacred. I spent some fifty years or more of my life in a country where no power could abrogate a contract without the consent of the parties interested. There is no such power vested in the president or in congress or in all the courts of the United States, nor can all these combined annul or modify in the slightest degree the contract rights of the humblest citizen of that republic. Contracts should be regarded as sacred. Now, western Canada and eastern Canada are interested in a contract-a contract that was paid for, a contract that has stood for nearly thirty years-and we in western Canada insist that that contract shall be duly recognized. I believe the people are entitled to that consideration. It is not a proper thing to tear up the contract without the consent of the people, and I submit that no man in this House has any mandate from their electors to destroy the Crowsnest pass agreement. We
Railway Freight Rates

from the west were instructed to see that it was reinstated, and we thought we had succeeded, but it has been so seriously modified by the Supreme court that it is hardly recognizable.
In the course of this debate yesterday it was said that the parties were willing to rescind this contract. I deny that assertion. The people of the west are not ready to rescind it, and they are the real parties in interest. They are clamouring against a re-scision, they are insisting that the contract be carried out and that the railroad company should be held to its agreement. It was suggested yesterday by the member for West Calgary (Mr. Shaw) that the Board of Railway Commisisoners were handicapped by the water rates and consequently were not able to raise the railway rates indiscriminately in the east. That is true no doubt. They are not only handicapped by that factor, but they are handicapped by another-a contract with the Canadian Pacific railway that the company shall have a 10 per cent dividend. That is one of the things they must insist on-and they seem very willing to insist on it. Now, where is that 10 per cent dividend to come from if freight rates cannot be raised in the east? It will come from the west. For that reason we need some safeguard, we have that safeguard in the Crowsnest pass agreement, and we insist on retaining it.
It is suggested that this arrangement does not give rates on westbound traffic to the Pacific coast. Of course it does not. But it does give to our British Columbia friends the right to ship their wheat to Fort William if they want to, there is no discrimination against them in that regard, and they can ship east under the agreement just as we do. So I say they are not discriminated against. Of course, statutory rates for westbound traffic could1 be enacted, but such rates are not favoured, and the rates under the Crows-.nest pass agreement are not statutory rates. It may be suggested that the agreement has been extended to take in additional territory since the Supreme court decision was rendered. That is true, but it is for the purpose of preventing discrimination. That decision merely *extends the Crowsnest pass rates to the territory where they were in force before the *agreement was tinkered with by the former government. Its application has been extended only as far as it extended prior to that catastrophe to our Crowsnest pass agreement. But that extension is not a fixing of rates; *the agreement fixes the rates; the Supreme court merely fixed the bounds of the extension.

Now, what position do we in the west find ourselves in? We are getting some things that we did not have; we are losing some things that we did have. We are losing the westbound rates on various commodities, and we deplore that fact. We insist that parliament has no right to do that thing, we insist that we are entitled to the Crowsnest pass agreement. But we are making a sort of trade it seems-not very willingly on our part. For instance, under the Supreme court decision there is not a point in my constituency that would derive a dollar's benefit from the Crowsnest pass agreement; we would not get it on the westbound nor on the eastbound traffic.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
The hon.
member states that we are trading. Is it true we are trading, or it is not rather that the trade is being tendered to us?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: It is being forced upon us. I repeat, under the Crowsnest pass agreement, as construed by the Supreme court, there is not a point in the Battleford constituency where we will have the benefit of one penny on the rates westbound or east-bound. The new arrangement on wheat and flour will extend to all points in that constituency, so that I am not sure but what we are getting a better trade. But I do not like the principle of it. I do not believe anybody has the right to take that agreement away from us without our consent. I therefore insist that we return to the Crowsnest pass agreement and1 make it applicable as it was before it was tinkered with by the former government. That is the position I think the government should take, and with that position the west will be entirely satisfied.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
One can usually depend
on getting the standard Liberal doctrine and Liberal argument from the hon. member for Battleford (Mr. McConica), but this evening he diverged. I cannot say that lie presented anything worse than what the government has presented from the beginning of this debate, but at last he broke his record and swerved a little from the straight and narrow path of the Liberal government. His tenderness for a contract is really pathetic. He never wants a contract broken unless it is in favour of himself, but then he is quite ready to weigh the merits of the change and assume the whole responsibility for it.
The railway rates question is before us again, and we have need to have it before us.
I do not think there ever was anything demanding solution more urgently than this

Railway Freight Rates
question has for many months gone by. It has seemed a very strange thing that while parliament was being served up with all sorts of little tinkering legislation and every manner of bill, oeeupying the time of the members week after week, the business of the country was allowed to wrestle with a condition of turmoil and chaos, and no remedy at all (provided. We had to wait till the very eve of prorogation, till within a few days of the close, to enable the government to come down with this legislation. All the facts for that legislation, all the data, were before them months ago. There was nothing they could possibly have been waiting for. All they were waiting for was a time fit and proper to try to get it through, and in their wisdom they considered the last hurried hours of the session would be the best.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: The Saskatchewan election may have been a factor.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
And I presume, as well,
the synchronism of the Saskatchewan election may have affected their politically-minded policies.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Where did I hear that
word before?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
I think it was from the
Minister of Railways.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: I think it was the Minister of Finance in my hon. friend's government.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is
a piece of floundering and irrational legislation. It had to be so. The government had to bring in something of this kind, or completely swallow the position they took two years ago. It is because they got into the mire two years ago that they have to come to parliament for legislation now, and it is because they are not willing to reverse an unsound step they took two years ago that they have to bring in legislation of this kind
I felt rather sorry for the Minister of Public Works (Mr. King) in the course of his speech. I do not think he made much of a presentation, but he did the best he could, and I do not know that anybody could have done any better who had been a minister and whose province had been treated by his colleagues the way the Minister of Public Works and his province have been treated in this legislation. I did not expect to see the radiant smile that we were told beamed over his countenance when interviewed by the newspaper reporter after the order in council which preceded this legislation was announced
to the public. The radiant smile I knew would not be there. Instead, he reminded me of nothing so much as a man trying to race as fast as he could through a bog, and the speed that he managed to acquire was not very much.
After all, there should not be any great difficulty for this parliament in determining its course as regards the railway rates. The policy of Canada was determined upon in this respect years ago. Always, ever since we have had a parliament, the right, of course, to fix rates, or to determine the principles upon which rates should be fixed, or both, has resided in the parliament of Canada in so far as Dominion railways are concerned. We have always had that. We could do it by legislation or by the creation of a body, a committee of the Privy Council or otherwise. We could do it through any agency we wished, or we could do it by bargain, if we liked, with the railway company. The jurisdiction has always been ours. The bargain with the railway company really meant, nothing, for the reason that whether the railway company consented or not, we always had power to enforce it by statute if we wanted. The control has been ours. The problem that faced us has been:	How should we exercise it?
First of all, it was exercised through a committee of the Privy Council for many years, enabled to do so by statute of parliament. This was changed in 1903, and a judicial body was created. That judicial body was entrusted, subject to certain underlying principles defined by parliament, to fix all rates in this country. That body, the railway commission, has functioned as a judicial body ever since. It functioned unhampered although there was existing an agreement that had not been removed, but an agreement that was quiescent, ineffective, because its terms had become obsolete and were not necessary for the day. The railway commission operated unhampered until this government came into power. Then pressure was brought to bear from a section of Canada to interfere, to alter the course which had been pursued. Conditions had arisen which brought into being again the bones of that old agreement, conditions which were due to the war-rising rates, rising costs, rising wages all over this country-and the agreement was suspended by the then government. It was a matter the disposal of which could wait, and well wait, more peaceful and quiet times. The suspension terminated in 1922, and then it was this government came upon the scene.
Railway Freight Rates

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Would the right hon.
gentleman assume that we have had a mandate from the people of Canada to change this contract?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
We have a mandate
from the people of Canada to do whatever is in the interests of the Canadian people. I have not started yet to argue whether it is in the interests of the Canadian people or
whether it is not; what I say is there has never been any vested right on the part of anyone in this contract the moment it appears that it is not in the interest of the whole people of Canada. That is all I have sought to convince this House of. If there were some other parties to the contract besides Canada on the one hand and the Canadian Pacific on the other-if there was a third party or a fourth party, then they would have rights too, but is theTe? If so, who is the third party? Canada is one, the Canadian Pacific is the other, who is the third? If any third party was in the contract at all he would have to show, first consideration; but there is no third party in it, there is nobody else a party to it at all. If the three western provinces had been in the consideration given then this parliament would have no right to set aside the contract except at the price of compensation to those provinces. But that is not the condition.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Would the statement or
assertion that the right hon. gentleman has made apply for instance to the Manitoba contract regulating rates, that was made with the old Canadian Northern Railway Company by the late Roblin government?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: No it would not apply; my argument would have no application whatever. Were I standing in the Manitoba legislature and arguing as to the duty of that legislature, I would argue just the same. I would say if the other party is ready to waive it, all you have to consider is the interests of the people of Canada. You can waive it as soon as you feel it is in their interests. But I cannot. I am in the parliament of Canada. The parties to that contract were the Canadian Northern and the government of Manitoba, and this parliament takes a very serious step when it wipes out a contract between other parties and assumes no responsibility for compensation.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
This was a bargain that
was made between the parliament of Canada and the Canadian Pacific Railway that was supposed to be in the interests of the three prairie provinces. Does not the hon. leader of the opposition believe that this parliament has some duty to see that these benefits are still conferred upon those provinces?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
This parliament's duty
is to the whole of Canada. Our duty is to the three prairie provinces just as much and just as directly as to any other provinces of the country. But the three prairie provinces, while they may have been the special beneficiaries of the original contract, were in
Railway Freight Rates

no way parties to the contract and had no special rights under it. They were special beneficiaries, perhaps, although the Minister of Public Works in his .desire to square himself with British Columbia, argued to-night, rather circuitously, I admit, that British Columbia was a beneficiary too; and indeed the Minister of Railways argued, likely for some similar purpose, that the rest of the country was a beneficiary. Perhaps in a sense everybody was a beneficiary. I frankly admit that the three prairie provinces were the principal beneficiaries. But the fact that this government enters into an arrangement especially beneficial to one party does not give that party a better right than all the rest of the country to review the general merits of the contract. Every part of this country has just the same right to review entirely the general merits from the standpoint of the whole people as have the representatives of the provinces of western Canada, and I am not saying this merely because I am standing now at a considerable distance from the taxoayers of those provinces. I have said this right on the plains, and I do not see for the life of me how any other line of reasoning can be followed.
Such is the position, as I understand it, of the contract itself. We have to consider, as we had to consider two years ago, whether it is in the interests of those for whom we are trustees, the whole people of this Dominion to maintain that contract as an integral and solemn pact. Is there one hon. member in this House who will suggest for one minute that it is? I am in the presence of men who I know would suggest it, if nothing restrained them except bashfulness and timidity. There is nobody who would suggest the enforcement of that contract, as the contract is now interpreted at least, and as the contract was understood by this House three years ago, though perhaps a different interpretation. In every aspect of this question, there is no member of this House who would suggest that you could enforce that contract in the interests of the people of Canada. The hon. member for North Battleford (Mr. Davies) says the contract has been so changed by the Supreme court that you cannot recognize it now at all. Whatever else we) may say about the hon. member for North Battleford, we can say for him that he has a mind of his own. He is not a lawyer, but has common-sense. I ask him, did he ever hear in his life of the courts changing a contract? That is not what the courts are for. If the Supreme court changed this contract, I think he had better set to work by some means or other

and get rid of the 'Supreme court. All the Supreme court had any right to do, and all it was asked to do was, to tell us what the contract meant. The Supreme court told us the contract meant such a thing and no more. For the hon. member to argue that we are justified in tinkering with its terms, and shutting this out or taking that in because it has been mutilated by the Supreme court, is to suggest something to this House that does no credit to his recognized intelligence. All we have now as the result of the government's action is a court decision as to what it means. I do not think we needed that decision. I do not think it mattered a whit whether the contract meant what the court said it meant, or whether the contract meant what the majority of the House said it meant two years ago. Taking it either one way or the other, you cannot enforce it in this country. The government, acting in the interests of the people, has to fall away from the contract and is bound to. It fell away two years ago when neither the government nor this House thought the contract had the strict interpretation which the Supreme court thought it had. The fact of the matter is that twenty-five years have so disturbed the current of trade in Canada, and have so altered the whole trend of prices in Canada, that the contract to-day is an absurdity. The contract to-day, instead of contributing to equalization, overthrows every possibility of equalization. It defies every principle on which any rate structure can be based. Is that true or is it an exaggeration? Nobody in the House has claimed otherwise. The Minister of Railways admits it. He expounds it. The Minister of National Defence did the same. I have heard member after member stand up and say the same thing. If that is the case, is it in the interests of the people of Canada that we stand on our rights under the contract? Surely now I am in a position where I can say that parliament is free. Surely I am now in the position where I can say that it is parliament's duty to turn its back upon that contract. The minister says, "Oh, we will keep part of it." Have we any right to keep a part of it and to throw the rest away? If so, where do we get the right? Whoever heard of a contractor assuming to himself the right to do what he liked with part of the contract and put the rest in the wastepaper basket?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Did the right hon. member anticipate this day of debate when he or his government allowed the suspension of the Crowsnest pass agreement under the War Measures Act?

Railway Freight Rates

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: No, we had no prophetic powers. I do not think we would have even prophesied that hon. members opposite would be in the treasury benches, but if we had so prophesied we would never have thought that they would have done this. We suspended the agreement in order that the whole question could be reviewed at a time when such questions would more appropriately come up.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Is it not a fact that parliament did, as far as they were concerned, abrogate the agreement, and the Senate said no?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: I have not heard of that. If that is history I have never read that portion of our history.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
I understood that the
Senate was the body that saved the contract and suspended it for three years.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
That may possibly be. It does not matter at all to the argument. That would only mean that the Senate decided there should be a time for review later. If so, it means that still less of the responsibility for the suspension instead of abrogation would rest on me, and to that extent I am grateful to the hon. gentleman from Strathcona for mentioning the matter.
I was dealing with that phase of the question as to our right to pick and choose among the clauses of the contract, and then to justify our conduct to-day in relation to that contract. I appeal to the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster), did he ever in his life hear of anything more absurd? It may be the duty of parliament to fix special rates in this House, and I will argue that in a minute. But for goodness' sake, if it is our duty to do so, let us manfully do it and do not let us get behind the shadow of a dead contract, a contract that we proclaim ourselves we cannot possibly adhere to and that the other party to the contract also wants to abandon.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: If the people of Canada had been satisfied with the right hon. gentleman's work as regards the suspension of the Crowsnest pass agreement and other things, would he not be back here as Prime Minister instead of as leader of the opposition?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: My mind is much in the same channel as that of the hon. member for Strathcona. That, I think, is also an irremediable disaster. I have come to the point now whether or not there are such circumstances as would make it the part of wisdom for this parliament to vary the course pursued for years and, in respect of certain commodities, to fix a certain rate. It would take, hon. gentlemen will admit, a very strong argument, to justify such a variation. It would take 'very extraordinary circumstances to justify it. I have tried to listen to those who contend that such is our duty. One says: It is essential for the west; we must have lower rates there in order to function. I know it is very essential for the west to have low rates, but I do not see that it is any more essential for them than it is for the Maritime provinces or for British Columbia to have low rates. It is essential for all of us to have low rates. Others say: Well, in the west we are not sure of low rates, because in the east they have water competition which is a factor in determining rates, and consquently there is likely to be too big a burden put upon us. You can point to similar conditions in all parts of Canada. You can point to many another part of this country where there is no water competition. Is parliament going to assume the duty of legislating rates in this House everywhere except where there is water competition? If we are not, how are we going to justify doing it for one section of the country?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Because of the volume of
freight in the west.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
There are undoubtedly
portions of the west to-day that, in my judgment, are paying under the Crowsnest pass agreement lower rates than they would pay otherwise, but the great part of the west, I believe, are not, and that is shown by the offer of the railways two years ago before the committee. The point is this:	If they are
not higher than is fair, than the railway commission would fix, why in the world are hon. gentlemen asking for the continuance of this agreement? Is not the railway commission competent to take these matters into consideration? Let me put the position in this way to hon. gentlemen. If some special consideration should be given to the absence of water competition, is it not the right and the proper function of parliament to declare what that consideration should be, to lay down a principle governing the matter, and to direct the railway commission to follow that principle? Is not that the right course for parliament to pursue?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: And what else does the Crowsnest agreement do?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: The Crowsnest agreement does not fix any principle; it is merely the application of a schedule fixed by parliament. It is a wholly different thing. This parliament might perhaps be moved to give to all portions of Canada which lack water competition some special advantage. Very well; declare that principle and embody it in your law. That is the function of parliament. But when a certain section come to the government and say, "We want you to fix rates along this schedule for us because we will not depend upon the railway commission, believing that the commission has no regard for our interests at all"-then hon. gentlemen cannot ask the representatives of other parts of the country to abide under the jurisdiction of a tribunal in which they have no confidence themselves.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Would the right hon. gentleman support that suggestion?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Well, I would need to
see how the law was put into effect. I have never subscribed to the suggestion, but I do say that those who subscribe to it, believing that the inland parts of Canada should have some special advantage, should see to it that this principle is embodied in our law and that the railway commission shall be instructed to apply it. That at any rate is the course they should advocate.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Would the right hon. gentleman argue that the people of the west had no need for concern after the action of the railway commission last fall in abrogating the Crowsnest agreement, in regard to which there was dissension among the members of the board itself?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
If the west has need
for concern because of any action the railway commission may have taken, then the whole of Canada should be concerned. Hon. gentlemen should be equally solicitous for other parts of the country as they are for themselves, and that is the contention I am advancing. Now, what is to be the attitude of hon. gentlemen towards the representatives of British Columbia? And I take British Columbia only by way of illustration. The Maritime provinces have just as insuperable and invincible an attack against the measure as has British Columbia, and I do not see how any member of this House can go to the Maritime provinces and defend before the people there a vote in support of this legislation. Here is British Columbia declaring, "You give our competitors to the east certain rates, while our rates are such and such a percentage higher. We now call upon you to give equal rates to these commodities going westward." And what does the government say in reply? They say, "Well, we have a pious aspiration in an order in council, and we have conveyed the same pious aspiration to the railway commission, that they will do something in the matter." The minister from that province has expressed a rather lively hope to-night that they will. But how is it that the representatives of British Columbia must rest on a mere pious aspiration while the representatives of three other provinces rest on solid law? Is that fair or just? Is that
Railway Freight Rates

going to contribute to the unity of the country? British Columbia under this legislation is worse off than it was before. When it comes before the railway commission now it is faced among other things -with the railway returns, wthich are affected by this pact. This pact now is extended over the whole northern area, and in the words of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald, Pictou) it is now three times what it was by law in the prairie provinces. By law, under this supposedly sacred contract, it covered only thirty-five per cent of what it does to-day, and therefore the whole earnings are affected. When therefore British Columbia comes before the commission it will be told that any reduction is impossible in view of these earnings.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Is the right hon. gentleman in favour of extending to British Columbia the privileges which we have under the Crowsnest pass agreement?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: I would extend them to the whole of Canada if we could beep the railways going; and so would the railway commission. It is easy for hon. members to get up and say that they are in favour of lower rates here and lower rates there. Hon. gentlemen are safe in doing so so long as they know they will not be in office. But those who are in office must keep the railways functioning.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: If the leader of the opposition looked at the matter fairly, would he not give British Columbia the same treatment as is given to other places?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: That is what I am pleading for.	'*

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
And that is what we are
ready to do.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
I say, do for British
Columbia what you do for any other part of the country. But if you cannot do it for British Columbia, for the Maritime provinces, for Quebec and Ontario, you should not do it for any other section of the Dominion.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Does the
hon. gentleman suggest that the rates in the Maritime provinces are higher than the Crowsnest rates in the west?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: If I were an expert on freight rates I should be on the railway commission and not here.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Will the
hon. gentleman take the word of the railway commission?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
I will take the word
of the railway commission for the facts as they relate to the west as well as to the east. The trouble is that hon. gentlemen are ready to take the railway commission as an authority for every part of Canada but their own. Again I address myself to the position of hon. gentlemen in relation to British Columbia. British Columbia will have to be denied redress; at least the denial will now be more forceful than ever .because of the extended effect of this agreement. Yet the minister from British Columbia wore a radiant smile, according to the newspapers, when he thought of the great victory he had achieved because of this legislation. Here is the order in council. It preceded the legislation in order that-its publicity would precede the publicity of the legislation; because the order in council has no virtue on earth except from the standpoint of publicity. It has no virtue at all except as propaganda; it is just so much eye-wash, just froth and foam. That is all it is. First of all it is a piece of literature and history; it recites the verdict of the court and all that sort of thing, and the only part that has even the appearance of meaning anything is the last page. I quote from that page the following:
The committee therefore advise that the board be directed to make a thorough investigation of the rate structures of railways and railway companies-
That "rate structures" is the new phrase of this government; it has supplanted all the other favourites that have done duty so long.
-subject to the jurisdiction of parliament, with a view to the establishment of a fair and reasonable rate structure, which will, under substantially similar circumstances and conditions, be equal in its application to all persons and localities, so as to permit of the freest possible interchange of commodities between the various provinces and territories of the Dominion and the expansion of its trade, both foreign and domestic, having due regard to the needs of its agricultural and other basic industries,-
How novel, how revolutionary that suggestion is.
-and in particular to:
(a)	The claim asserted on behalf of the Maritime provinces that they are entitled to the restoration of the rate basis which they enjoyed prior to 1919;
(b)	The encouragement of the movement of traffic through Canadian ports;
(c)	The increased traffic westward and eastward through Pacific coast ports owing to the expansion of trade with the Orient and to the transportation of products through the Panama canal.
Do hon. gentlemen get the full effect of that? The government says to the railway commission, "We have tied your hands to a certain section of the Crowsnest pass agreement; we have tied them by an act of parliament.

Railuxiy Freight Rates
Now we tell you to go to work and devise a fair and reasonable rate structure; and when you are doing that, you might be good enough to have regard to the claim asserted by those representing the Maritime provinces that they have certain rights." Is there any principle there defined upon which the railway commission can act? None whatever. There is just a dodging of principle, that is all. Having regard to a claim asserted-no expression that there is anything in the claim, not a suggestion of it. Does anybody imagine that they have not had regard to that claim before? What is next?
Having regard to the necessity of encouraging the movement of traffic through Canadian ports.
If there is a member of the commission that has failed to have regard to that in all his work up to date, then the statute should be repealed so that he could be got rid of and another commissioner appointed in his place. The same is true of the last paragraph. Have we had a lot of dullards in the railway commission that they did not know there was a Panama canal, that there was now more traffic westward? It is all right to lay down a principle and tell the railway commission, "Now, go and investigate your rate structure and make it conform to that principle." That as done in 1920. In the judgment of the railway commission of that time they declared they based their decision in part on the necessities of the National railways. We did not tell them to go back and review their decision in the light of the fact that the National Railways were in heavy debt or were built before their time; we told them to go back and review their finding in the light of our declaration that they had to leave the National Railways out altogether. There we declared a principle and took the responsibility ourselves. A reference back on a principle clearly defined means something; but here they define nothing. The railway commission has for twenty years been instructed to investigate the rate structure to make it fair and reasonable and produce equalization as far as possible. And that is all that it is instructed to do here. All this order in council means to the railway commission is simply this:	You, the railway commission of Canada, now set to work and do what you have been told to do for the last twenty years. This is supposed to be consolation to British Columbia and to the Maritime provinces. They are told to rejoice and be glad over the empty words of a futile order in council, while in order to get enough votes in parliament the representatives of 282
those districts are told to go back and rely on rates fixed by this House. Now, is this law, it is equity, is it common sense? I appeal again to the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster). There is no answer?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: I am not a member of the railway commission.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
No, but he is a member o( parliament, and he has to come to a decision as to this. How can he as a Liberal -who loves that name at least, whatever he may think of the record-how can he vote for legislation that denies every principle of Liberalism, or so-called Liberalism, that has not a particle of equity in any line of it? If any hon. member thinks there is any consolation for his district, unless he comes from the special one, I should like to find how he is going to establish it. All the rest of Canada is told, "Go back and take what solace you can out of these words of the order in .council"-words that have been repeated over and over again for twenty- three years, words that in effect were in the original law, words that to-day are not supplemented by any declaration of principle at all. The w'hole thing is just a waste of printer's ink in order that a good taste could be put in the mouth of British Columbia and the Mari-times before this inequitable legislation was brought down.	*
There is only one course parliament should have pursued years ago, it should have met the problem right face forward and acted upon the sound, safe principle of doing the same for every part of Canada. Then there would have been no trouble to-day. Does anybody imagine that this is going to end the problem? It cannot. I do not care whether the railway rates of the Crowsnest pass agreement are lower or higher than the average level of Canada, so far as this argument is concerned, as long as you have to get a maximum fixed by parliament for one section, while the other sections are denied it, you cannot have good feeling in this country, you cannot have the sentiment among the people that they are fairly treated at the hands of parliament. Whether those rates are higher or lower, the people of the Maritimes, being people of the same composition as the rest of us, are bound to believe that they are under a special disadvantage because parliament would not do for them what it has done for the prairies. They are bound to believe it anyway, and you cannot possibly find any fault with them for so believing. I ask hon. members from the prairie provinces, suppose this legislation were for the Maritimes, and were denied to them,

would they like to have the members from those provinces stand up and say, "Oh, but we have to have certain rates or we cannot function. These rates are not lower than you are paying out in the west, we assure you they are not." Would hon. members from the west take that for an answer? Not one.

speechtext:
It will 'be
time enough to raise the maximum when the other rates are up to the general level.
' Mr. MEIGHEN: Very good. If the position were reversed, and we were fixing maximum rates for the Martime provinces, and some member from the Maritime should stand up and tell him, "Oh, we are fixing these maximum rates, but they are not a bit lower than yours," I should like to hear what he would say. He would get up and say, "Very well, go and fix the other rates. If you want to go to the commission, go yourselves." Would not that be his answer?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
