speechtext:
We are not fixing the
rates; they were fixed about twenty-seven years ago.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: I got past that argument about three-quarters of an hour ago. Perhaps I had not awakened the hon. member at that time. We are fixing rates in this legislation, and this talk about an agreement is simply concealing ourselves behind an imaginary barrier.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Is it not a fact that the Conservative government in 1916 set a special rate on grain from Armstrong to Quebec?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
I have no recollection
of the event at all, and I am quite satisfied we did not set any rate. But in war time there are occasions when very quick action is necessary that would not be considered in peace time at all. But I do not think any special rate was fixed by the government at that time.	.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Did I understand the
right hon. gentleman to say that his government suggested to the Board of Railway Commissioners that in considering the rates they should have special regard for the condition of the National Railways?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
No, we said the very
contrary. We said, "A great mileage of the Canadian National Railways is premature, a

great deal of it was built, not for commercial profit as was the Canadian Pacific 'railway, but for colonization or other advantages"- that was a euphemism, we did not want to put in the order in council that it was purely for winning elections, so we stated it that way -"and as a consequence it is not fair to the shippers of Canada to-day to load on them the cost of that error; the whole of Canada should bear it. Therefore, come to your decisions wholly without regard to what the necessities of the National Railways may be."

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my contribution to the discussion will be brief. It is prompted only by the desire to see a solution of this vexed problem that shall be reasonably satisfactory to all concerned. Yesterday the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) reviewed the provisions of the Crowsnest pass agreement and the whole course of events leading up to the present situation, and therefore I shall not take the time of the House by going over the same ground again. The outstanding point, in the present debate is that the decision of the Supreme court has left a condition of discrimination so far as freight rates are concerned which is intolerable, and must be remedied. We have, now, to consider ways and means of removing that discrimination. It seems to me that that can be done in any one of three ways: First, to make the Crowsnest rates on the various commodities applicable on all parts of the railways; second, to restore the general rates and abolish discrimination in that way; and third, to give the railway board of Canada a free hand to make such rates as they think are equitable and in the interests of the whole of Canada.
Before going on to discuss these various methods, I should like to say that I believe that special agreements made in the interest of any particular section of the country or of any class of the people, are bad as a matter of policy. I think possibly that might be modified in some cases by the fact that the national interest might be served by a modification of the principle, especially in such a country as Canada, where we have such a diversification of interests that compromise sometimes is necessary. We have, for example, our friends immediately opposite frequently saying that the tariff is a matter of class legislation, and for that reason should not be tolerated. That is combated by a good many members of this House, who say that it is not class legislation, that the tariff is beneficial to the whole of Canada, and for that reason should be continued. Whether it be class legislation or not, it might be held

Railway Freight Rates
to be in the public interest. On the other hand, we have now a proposal from our friends opposite, and I think from the government, that we should enact legislation by way of granting the privilege of rural credits, which might be argued to be in the nature of class legislation,, but which may be desirable in the public interest.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: I am sure the hon. member does not wish to mislead the House. Perhaps he is not aware of the fact that the rural credits legislation suggested will place no burden on the taxpayers of the Dominion, but will rest only with the provinces that take advantage of it.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Perhaps my illustration was not very good, but I think the House will readily see the point I am trying to make. Admitting therefore, as I do, and as I think all will, that class legislation is bad, that special agreements for the advantage of any one section of the country are bad, and also that the matter of freight rate making should not be given to parliament, we have then to consider, so far as I see the question, how far we should depart in the public interest from the principle I laid down, that rate making should not be given to parliament but should remain vested in the Board of Railway Commissioners.
The hon. leader of the Progressives spoke yesterday of the solemn contract of the Crowsnest agreement, and said that because it was a solemn contract, it should be maintained. Now I must take issue with him, and with my hon. friend from Battleford, who stated that that contract cannot be varied without the consent of the western people, and I think the members of the House will believe me when I say that I do that without any animosity whatever towards the people of western Canada. It should be remembered, and I agree in this with the right hon. leader of the official opposition, that that contract was made between the government of Canada, or the parliament of Canada, if you like, and the Canadian Pacific Railway. The consideration for the contract that was given to the Canadian Pacific Railway, something like $3,600,000,-was paid by the people of Canada. I contend that when both parties to an agreement decide and mutually agree to vary or even to abolish a contract entirely, they have a perfectly legal and a moral right so to do. So I do not think this House should be deterred because of the fact that a contract did exist.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Nobody denies those facts.
282-i

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: I am of the opinion that he said it was a solemn contract and therefore should not be tampered with, or words to that effect.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Would not the hon. member also argue that the Board of Railway Commissioners should have approached both parties to the contract before they abrogated *the Crowsnest rates last fall, instead of just *taking the Canadian Pacific side of the case?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: I do not think it is right to accuse the Board of Railway Commissioners of taking the Canadian Pacific side of it. I am perfectly willing, although perhaps I have not sublime confidence in the board, to give them credit for trying to do what is right, although possibly they may be mistaken in some of their judgments.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Does not the hon. member consider that this agreement was made for the benefit of the western provinces, to guarantee them against paying too high a freight rate?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
I will say that the people of the western provinces were perhaps the chief beneficiaries under the agreement, but not the sole beneficiaries. They were not specifically parties to this agreement. It was an agreement between the government of *Canada and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.
I would like to refer to the work done by the committee appointed by parliament in 1922, a committee of twenty-five members of this House, who were to make a report to parliament as to whether the Crowsnest agreement should be allowed to come into force or whether its suspension should be continued. I had the honour of being a member of that committee, and that is why I refer to it now. It is no secret to say that I believe the disposition of the majority of the members of that committee was to allow all the rates on the commodities mentioned in the Crowsnest pass agreement, grain included, to be referred to the railway board, and that a new freight rate structure should be framed.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Following up my first
question, does not the hon. member think it is only reasonable for the western provinces t.o want to know what they are going to get before they give up the bargain they have already got?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
The western provinces have only such a bargain as the parliament of Canada in agreement with the Canadian Pacific Railway sees fit to give them. They have
Railway Freight Rates

what they have only by reason of a contract made between the government of Canada and the Canadian Pacific.
If I may get back to the work of that committee, there was a feeling in that committee that in theory at least the whole matter of rate making should be vested in 11 p.m. the railway commission, but there were some of us, and I was one of them, -who felt that in the interests of harmony, in the interests of the country in general, and in the interests of the western people, we might depart to some extent from that principle, and for that reason we advocated and secured that the freight rates on grain and flour should be allowed to come into force according to the terms of the Crowsnest agreement. I say frankly, Mr. Chairman, that I have sometimes within the last few days almost felt that we made a mistake. I am not going to say that definitely, because I have felt that we were reasonable at that time in what we did. But I do say that the proposal made by the government to allow the Crowsnest rates on grain and flour to remain in force, and to widen tremendously the scope and the application of those rates, is such a concession that our friends opposite should support it unanimously and without any objection. I say frankly that I am disappointed at the attitude taken by some of my very good friends opposite in insisting that the whole list of commodities should be restored so far as the Crowsnest pass rates are concerned. Now some of the members of that committee in 1922 compromised pretty heavily. They declared themselves in favour of retaining the Crowsnest pass rates on grain and flour. Some of us to some extent sacrificed the interests of our own constituencies in so doing; I know there is one member of the committee, I do not see him in the chamber just now, and I am another one-who sacrificed the Crowsnest pass rates on commodities manufactured in his constituency. I refer to furniture. Furniture is one of the commodities mentioned in the Crowsnest pass agreement. We were quite willing to forego the lower rates on furniture and to give to the west the benefits of the lower rates on grain and flour because we felt at the time that the west had difficulties to contend with and that we could stand the reduction a little better than they could. At any rate we did that in what we thought was in the national interest.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Might I suggest to my hon. friend that that suspension on furniture and other articles was only for two years.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Just for one year.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: It was only for one year and could be renewed for another year. I may add that at that time we were under the impression that if the Crowsnest pass agreement came into force in its entirety that furniture would get the benefit of the lower rate. However, what we did we did in good faith so far as giving the rates on flour and grain are concerned. Unfortunately in my own case we never got the benefit of the reduced Crowsnest pass rates on furniture.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Who does my hon. friend think pays the freight on a carload of furniture going from his town to any point in the west?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
That is an old question
which I think the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) answered this afternoon. I have no doubt the westerner pays the freight but I will also say this-that every reduction of freight on a commodity surely assists the sale of that commodity if the price is lowered. But we did not anticipate at that time any such decision as was given later, that the Crowsnest pass rates on furniture and other commodities would apply only to such points as were in existence on the Canadian Pacific Railway in 1897. Because of that, my own city-and I may say that in the constituency which I represent we have about twenty-five furniture factories-we do not get the benefit of the Crowsnest pass rates on furniture, and to give you an idea of the discrimination that exists I shall merely quote by way of example, the rate we have to pay in competition with furniture manufacturers in the city of Woodstock, situated about thirty miles from Kitchener. Woodstock got the benefit of the Crowsnest pass rates of 1897 on furniture to Winnipeg of 86J cents per hundred pounds, whereas from Kitchener to Winnipeg the rate is $1.38 per hundred pounds, an increase over the Woodstock rate of a little over sixty per cent. Our furniture manufacturers, however, are resourceful enough to circumvent that. They bill their goods to the city of Galt, about twelve miles away, and pay that extra rate. Galt was on the Canadian Pacific in 1897 and by shipping from that city they get the benefit of the Crowsnest pass rates. This does not work out so badly, but I assure you our manufacturers consider it is a very great nuisance and an unfair discrimination.
Now, if such a contract as the Crowsnest pass agreement were to be made to-day in the light of the fact that a railway commission exists, one of whose functions is the fixing of rates that are not discriminatory,

Railway Freight Rates
then I would say that the making of such a compact to-day would be in violation of the principles that I believe in that rates should not be made by parliament but should be made by a properly constituted body.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Did not the government propose to fix rates under the Petersen contract if it had gone through?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Well my answer to that
would be that, under the report submitted to the House the Petersen contract did not come into force. I would also say further-

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Would my hon. friend
just let me straighten that out.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Certainly.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Under the Petersen contract the government took the power to control the rates through any machinery it liked. That machinery would probably have been the Board of Railway Commissioners.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
If that explanation is not
satisfactory I will add this. I have already admitted, and I say now, that conditions may arise in this country that will make it advisable that we should sometimes vary and depart from any strict principle that may be laid down in matters of this kind. The leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Eorke), gave as the reason why we should go further in the making .of rates in this House, the fact that we are continuing rates that were made under the Crowsnest pass agreement. I do not consider that an entirely fair argument. The rates which are now given under the Crowsnest pass agreement on grain and flour are a concession to our western friends, one that I have already justified and can continue to justify under the proposal that is made now. My hon. friends should not take that as a reason why we should decide to go further in the violation of what I consider is a principle.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Wherein does the concession arise?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: In that it is a special agreement in which rates are given that are lower than normal rates and beyond which the railway commission is not able to go. They are specially fixed fey parliament and are below the regular rates. That is my argument.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: If it is a concession given in the case of the eastbound rates on grain and flour, is it not a burden on the western people that by raising the rates on the commodities going west they have to pay more when they come to buy those commodities?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
If -the rates are raised on
the other commodities going west-and there is as yet no ground for believing that will be the case, these rates are to go to the railway commission. We do not know that as a consequence they will be; it is not saddling the western people with anything that is not being borne equally by the other citizens of Canada.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has
not answered my question. If the rates are raised on goods going west and those rates are charged in the price we pay for the goods, is that not a burden On the west?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
I do not think I am called
upon to answer hypothetical questions. I may say, however, that I do not think there is any discrimination in that way. Westerners would simply be placed on the same footing as are all the other citizens of Canada.
We have had a good deal of argument as to whether tates in western Canada are generally higher than they are in the east. I know that when I come to discuss that question I am liable to meet opposition and perhaps enter on debatable ground.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: What does the hon. gentleman mean by "concession?"

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: I was hoping I had got away from that phase of the subject.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Does he mean it is an act of pure generosity on the government's part, or does the observation apply to some right we have in the west?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Well I would answer that
in this way: I believe that the west has no inherent right to receive such a concession, but I also believe that it may be in the public interest, it may be in the general interest of Canada, that western Canada should have some concessions that will enable them to make progress and to prosper and thus benefit the whole of Canada.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Does the hon. gentleman
mean by "concession" that we are getting a. service which is rendered at less than cost?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
I was coming to that point in a few minutes. However, I will answer my hon. friend briefly, yes.
I was beginning to discuss the question of rates. It is said the rates in western Canada are higher than in eastern Canada. The leader of the! Progressive party yesterday quoted a good many figures to prove that statement. I could, if I so desired, quote figures which would show that on similar
Railway Freight Rates

distances on internal points in the central provinces rates are higher than for similar distances on internal points in western Canada. I am not going to do that, and I would simply leave it with this observation, that our freight rate structure is such that you would be able to prove almost anything from the rate figures.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: If they are higher, they must be very high, because the internal rates in the west are high.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: I can show the hon. member a statement in regard to it in black and white, but I will not trouble the House with it now. I Shall leave that point with the statement that in northern Ontario, for example, rates are a good deal higher in many instances for similar distances within the province from Toronto, say, to some point in northern Ontario, than for similar distances in western Canada. That being the case, would my hon. friend argue that special agreements should be made in the interests of people living in northern Ontario? If we do that, where are we going to end? Because the same sort of thing will crop up in different parts of Canada. If these rates are not equitable, sureiy we should be able to trust the fixing of rates to the body properly constituted for that purpose. Something has been said about the fixing of rates in Ontario on the basis of water competition. To be quite frank, I have not attached so much importance to that as have some ethers. There is no doubt water competition has a good deal to do with the fixing of rates in Ontario, but there are many points in Ontario which are not affected by water competition at all. There may be competition along the water front, but in the interior of Ontario that does not apply. I would add this further: Is it reasonable that those who happen to live in such communities as have advantages because of their geographical location must . necessarily be expected to give up any of those advantages for the sake of those who happen not to be so advantageously situated? I am not sure that it is correct to say that because a certain rate is given, we will say in Ontario, in a thickly populated district, so much per mile or so much per hundred pounds for sc many miles, that absolutely the same rate must prevail in another portion of the country where traffic is less dense.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
No one
suggested that.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
That suggestion was made by another hon. member. We have an illustration of that in Ontario. As hon. members
[Mr Euler.]
know, Ontario has gone into the development of Niagara power. The municipalities that are nearest the source of supply get the lowest rates, and the other municipalities more remote from the Niagara district do not think that they should receive as low a rate as is enjoyed by the municipalities close to Niagara falls, because the cost of carrying that power to the municipalities more distant is greater than in the other case. I have heard of one or two complaints during the regime of Hon. Mr. Drury, when the suggestion was made that there should be a flat rate all over Ontario, but that proposition was never entertained.
I would lay down this definite principle, so far as rates are concerned: that we must have rates throughout Canada that will enable the railways to live.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Of course if you provide that the Railway board is the only authority to fix rates we cannot say any more; that settles that part of it, but do you not think the fact that the products of the central provinces have to be transported 1.000 miles either out or in requires some consideration? These provinces are not self-contained in any way. Everything they use has to be taken in, and everything they sell has to be taken out, and these provinces should have some consideration over other provinces differently situated.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
I am quite willing to agree
with my bon. friend as to that. It is a question how far we can go. I would be quite willing to agree that the rates on grain and flour should be according to the Crowsnest pass agreement, and I think that is a very considerable concession, if I may use that word without getting into trouble. But to say that we should carry the making of rates on all the commodities that might be mentioned into parliament, I think would be very inadvisable indeed.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: I was going to remark that the hon. member is evidently unaware that the Prime Minister positively stated on his tour in the west last fall that water competition was a factor in the fixing of railway rates.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
I have not contended that it had no bearing at all. I said I did not believe it had quite the importance that was sometimes attached to it. It has been claimed that western railway business is very profitable, and the inference is that the west is being discriminated against in favour of the east. Now if I may do so without arousing undue antagonism, I should like to say a few words

Railway Freight Rates
in regard to that. I have not any extensive figures with regard to the Canadian Pacific Railway, but I have it on very good authority -almost as good authority as one can get- that so far as the transportation of grain in western Canada by the Canadian Pacific Railway is concerned, their operating expenses are 98 per cent of their revenues; that they make money on the short haul, but lose money on the long haul. That leaves a margin of only 2 per cent. That margin of 2 per cent does not nearly cover the fixed charges and overhead which must be taken into account when you arrive at the net profit, so that the statement is made that the carrying of grain even ;by the Canadian Pacific Railway is not profitable.
Coming to the National Railways, the figures have been quoted before and have been questioned, but I have not yet seen them disproved. In the central region, in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, the figures show an operating profit last year of $16,433,446.96. The United States division showed a profit of $5,480,162.25. The western region showed an operating loss of $1,124,353.49, and the Atlantic region showed an operating loss of $3,545,004.24. These are either operating profits or operating losses, without taking into consideration, as I said before in the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway, the overhead or fixed charges. The president of the National Railways, before the committee on National Railways and Shipping not very long ago, made the statement-and hon. members have probably read it in the account of proceedings-that the Canadian National Railways lost money on every bushel of grain shipped eastward. That was an important [DOT] statement, made by an authority and deserves some consideration. I might add also that something has been said at times with regard to rates in the United States-

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
I would like to clear up
that point. I understood my hon. friend to say that the chairman of the National Railways said that the railway lost money on every bushel of grain shipped eastward. Was that from Fort William eastward, or from prairie points to Fort William?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: , Shipped eastward from any point in the prairie provinces, I think.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
I think the hon. member
for North Waterloo saw the statement of President Beatty at New York, that if the Canadian Northern had been content with their prairie lines to Fort William, they would have been the richest men and the richest railway in the world to-day.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Did he say that they would
make the money out of carrying grain or by selling land?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
The hon. member cannot
get away from it like that.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: I do not know. I have not seen the statement.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: The hon. member was speaking about the deficit on the western lines and, of course, that includes all those fool lines that were built by authority of this parliament and for which the west is not to blame, such as the line running up to Prince Rupert the operation of which must entail great loss and the duplication of lines throughout the west-lines that were never needed.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: The Hudson Bay railway.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: No. The Hudson Bay railway paid for itself. You cannot charge that up to the western lines. If you take just the prairie division where they are performing a useful function, they are paying institutions.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: I am quite willing to accept that observation, but I have never at any time heard that the westerners disapproved any of those lines while they were being built.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: This parliament must assume the responsibility for them.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Very well. I am coming a
little later to figures, which do not include the line running to Prince Rupert-which deal entirely with grain and which figures, I think, are quite authoritative. I was going to quote here some figures which I have with regard to rates in the United States.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: If the hon. member's statement is correct-and I am accepting it as correct-that there is a deficit on the National railways at the present time in moving grain eastward, is it not foolish to vote $5,000,000 for the Quebec harbour?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
I am sure the committee
does not expect me to go into a debate on the merits of the Quebec harbour.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
The point is there just the
same.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
It is stated by the National
railway authorities that if the general rates that now apply on the Great Northern railway in the United States were applied to the
Railway Freight Rates

National railways in western Canada, the revenues, and consequently, the operating profits, would be 820,473,000 greater than they were.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Is that on the same volume of grain?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
I have been fairly patient,
I think, and I will give the hon. member an opportunity in a moment. It is also stated that if the rates on the Northern Pacific were applied to the National railways-and this applies to general traffic-the revenues and consequently the operating profits would have been $24,608,000 greater than they were, an amount sufficiently large, if added to the operating profits which the National railways actually had last year, to pay the fixed charges to the general public.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Was that in 1924?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: What does the hon. member think would have happened to the men who were paying those rates?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
A little later I will give
hon. gentlemen the reason for my making these remarks. I might say now that I am not giving these citations in order to advocate that rates in western Canada should be increased. That is not my purpose at all.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Has the hon. member the
figures showing the quantity moved by the railways in the United States?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
I have not. I merely have
the net results. The revenue in the western region of Canada in 1924 on all commodities other than grain averaged 11.23 mills per ton-mile. If grain were included, then those revenues shrink to the astonishing figure of 7.63 mills per ton-mile as compared with the central region of 11.12 mills per ton-mile for all traffic. Those are official figures, and I think they would tend at least to confirm the view that grain is being carried at a loss. The operating loss on the Nationals, as was given this afternoon, on grain in western Canada was in 1923, $6,000,000. I am giving it just in round numbers. Last year, in 1924, the operating loss on grain was $5,812,000. I would draw attention to this significant fact, because it goes to prove what I have said before, that when less grain was carried-because less was carried in 1924 than in 1923- the loss was slightly less. I am going to leave that rather disagreeable subject, because I admit that I dislike to mention facts that are unpalatable to my western friends.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Was that loss occasioned
on the western division or the eastern division, because the hon. gentleman must remember that there are two rates?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
My information gives that
as being a loss sustained on the western division. I am not giving these figures, showing that railway business in western Canada is not profitable, and certainly not so far as grain is concerned to urge an increase of western rates, but I give them to impress, if possible, on my hon. friends opposite that, after all, the proposal which is made in this bill is a very generous one and one which, it seems to me, ought to be accepted without much protest.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: In reference to the matter that the hon. member is speaking about, has he seen a report that was distributed, I think, to nearly every member of parliament, by the Canadian Pacific, that rates allowed to our western people were nine cents per bushel less to the head of the lakes than rates that are allowed by the United States railways to the American farmers? I have a copy of it.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: I have not seen that particular statement, but I have seen a similar one which shows that rates in the western states are a good deal higher than they are in Canada.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
We have heard that for
years.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
If my figures are correct,
then under the proposal that is at present before the committee the government maintains losing rates on grain in the interest of the producers of western Canada. That means a great deal. It is giving more under the proposal that is now before the committee than was enjoyed by western Canada formerly, because, as has been stated by the Minister of Railways, it extends the scope of the application of those rates two-fold. The application of Crow rates is extended to all lines now in existence, both Canadian Pacific and Canadian National, and as well, I presume, to all lines that will be constructed in the future unless a change is made later on with regard to grain rates.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
I think the hon. member
said that the president of the National Railways stated that they had lost money on every bushel of grain hauled eastward. Did he make a similar statement with regard to grain hauled westward?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
He did not. He said that
he makes a little money on grain hauled westward.

Railway Freight Rates

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Would the hon. member be
willing to give his opinion whether the farmers of Alberta should not have a similar rate westward to that which they have eastward?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
I would say this, that I do
not like the idea that there should be any discrimination. If it is at all possible-I should like to see the same rates from the prairies to Pacific ports, proportionately speaking, as those that apply on grain going to the east. If these are facts as I have stated them, I want to repeat this, that I think our friends opposite ought to appreciate what is proposed in the legislation now before the House. Discrimination must be removed. I do not believe there is one hon. member in the Progressive party who will say otherwise. We have in Ontario a condition of affairs that is, perhaps, not fully appreciated by our hon. friends from the west, but it cannot be allowed to continue. Who shall remedy it? There is only one unbiased body in this country, a body specially created for that particular work. That body is the Board of Railway Commissioners, and one of its most important functions is the fixing of rates.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
The hon.
gentleman suggests that discriminations should be abolished. Does he mean discrimination as between different territories in the west, or does he mean that in so far as it is possible for the railway commission to do so, the general level of rates east and west ought to be the same.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: I do not know that I can go into any extended argument on that point. I say that there should be no unfair discrimination against any interest or any class of people, or any industry or commodity, east or west, north or south, or in any other direction. I stated at the outset that I believed in the principle that all rates should be fixed by the railway board and not by the parliament of Canada. We are departing to some extent from that principle inasmuch as we are allowing by act of parliament the continuance of the Crowsnest rates on grain and flour. But I am willing to compromise to that extent, and I am doing so for the same reason as influenced me in 1922 as a member of the committee; I feel that reduced rates on grain will be in the interests of harmony as well as in the interests of the country as a whole.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
If the hon. member is agreeable to having these preferential rates on wheat and flour, why not extend them to live stock, which are grain-fed? Why not
extend the principle further if you extend it at all?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: I am free to admit that I may be open to a charge of inconsistency in violating the principle I have laid down; but it is merely a matter of the degree to which we think it advisable to go in matters of this kind. I do not desire to go any further ini violation of that principle than we have already gone in the legislation now pending.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Does the hon. member not think it would be better to have the rates apply to live stock?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: If it is advisable to make a concession in relation to grain and flour it might be advisable to do the same thing in the case of live stock. But possibly somebody would want the rates applied to building material or agricultural implements or other articles. The varying of the principle cannot be carried too far.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Certainly.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: There are occasions when it may be in the interests of the country and of good business-I am not going to say good politics, because I do not care much about that-to depart from a too strict adherence to any particular principle.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: It shall be counted to you for righteousness.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: machinery, which ordinarily is in the same rate classification as agricultural implements, carries a rate of about $1.08 per hundred pounds from Toronto to Winnipeg. The manufacturers-or rather the consumers, we will say, because it is argued that the consumers pay the freight-might very well say, " Why should we be discriminated against in favour of the users of agricultural implements? That is only one instance. Coal oil is another. The Crow rate from Toronto to Winnipeg is 65J cents, but coal oil ordinarily is in the same rate classification as all other oils; yet all other oils are required to pay a rate of $1.14. Would that not constitute discrimination?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: How could it be discrimination when these articles are covered by special agreement made in 1897?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
We are not recognising the agreement of 1897 now; henceforward the conditions will be different. But suppose we consider the suggestion that these articles that are now in the Crowsnest agreement should all be restored and the Crowsnest rates made applicable all along the line, on all lines of railway. What would happen? You would immediately have requests from those shipping similar articles and who were being charged a higher rate, for equal treatment and you could not fairly refuse them the same rates. So that the whole situation bristles with difficulties that may not be at present apparent to hon. members.
The railway board is charged with the duty of making rates fair and equitable to all. We have set up the board to do that work. Why then not let the board perform that duty? They are infinitely better qualified to make these rates than are members of parliament. If parliament has no confidence in the railway board-and that sentiment has been expressed by some hon. members-then the remedy is not to throw the business of rate-making into this House; the remedy is so to constitute your board that you will have confidence in it.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: Why not give the board full control over the whole matter, if that is the hon. member's opinion?

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: I have answered that question already.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext: But you are approving of this bill.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
Yes, and I have already
stated my reason for so doing. In conclusion, I would appeal to my hon. friends opposite, for whose needs we on this side of the House have the greatest sympathy, to accept the

Mr. Chairman, the ground has been well covered, but as a representative of Winnipeg I feel I must join with other western members in protesting against the proposal contained in the bill now before us. Urgent appeals have been made that we should view this from a national standpoint. I submit that any truly national policy is dependent upon its meeting the needs of every section of the community. The people of the west feel that this measure will not meet their needs. I believe that measures of this kind are the sledge hammer blows that are driving the wedges that are separating the various parts of Canada. I cannot but utter a warning to the government from another angle altogether to that taken by the leader of the opposition

if measures oi this kind are persisted in you cannot expect to maintain a united Canada. We all pleac for unity, but that unity is possible onl>
under certain conditions. The existence oi the west is dependent almost entirely upon proper transportation. Those who have lived all their lives in the east perhaps can hardly realize how different the west is in this regard. Here for a hundred years communities have lived more or less self-contained, their markets to a considerable extent close at hand. But without transportation the west would still be in the control of the Indians; and if we do not give suitable transportation

Railway Freight Rates
rates the west might as well revert to the Indians. Make freight rates prohibitive and you strangle our agriculture. The markets of the west are not local markets. We are told again and again that it is well that we should build up industries in order that we might have local markets. Suppose we should attempt to do that in the west where would the east be under those circumstances? The people of the east are dependent upon the west, to a certain extent at least, for their markets, but those markets are available only so long as we are able to ship large quantities of foodstuffs overseas. I repeat, our western markets are not local, and that should be taken into consideration
This bill deprives the west, as has been repeated again and again, of certain statutory guarantees. And this is the main objection -it offers no satisfactory guarantees in return. It leaves the west to the tender mercies of the railway commission. Now, we may as well frankly recognize that the west has to a considerable extent lost confidence in that commission as now constituted. It is not merely a question of personnel. It is based on the fact that the commission is very largely working on principles which cannot continue to be applied if the west is to prosper. The commission is located more or less in the east, it is subject to the principles and ideals pertaining to this part of the country-principles and ideals which no doubt are held by the majority in Canada-and thus it cannot jbe expected to formulate policies that will meet the needs of the west.

One or two of
these points I should like to mention. We all appeal to general principles, and no one is more fond of doing so than my good friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster). The trouble is that people who hold the most diverse views and advocate the most adverse policies may appeal to the same general principles. The whole matter is one of the application of those principles. For instance, at the present time we hear a good deal about equalization. We all say, if we could only have equalization-whatever that means-we
would all be happy. But what do we mean by equalization? As soon as we begin to define it we are all at sixes and sevens again. As I have heard this word repeated so often, I have thought of the little story that is familiar to many of us of the old Scotch lady, who returned from church greatly edified. On being asked the cause of her elation, she answered, "'Oh, it was the sough of that blessed word Mesopotamia." I am inclined to believe that the government is trying to lull the country into a sense of -false security by repeating frequently enough that remarkable word-equalization.
The hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) has pointed out to-day that this bill makes no provision whatever for equalization of rates as between provinces. I submit we might very well go further than the demand of the -hon. member for Mackenzie. The hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) hardly likes to admit that geographical location ought to have any very great weight in the determining of freight rates. I submit that it is not an unheard of principle that geographical location should very decidedly determine rate policies. Let me give a very simple illustration. We are all supposed to be here on equal terms. When I come from Winnipeg my fare is paid by the government; the fare of the member for Skeena (Mr. Stork) is also paid by the government; but his fare is very different from mine, and mine is very different from that of a member from Montreal. However, the arrangements are made in such a way as, approximately at least, to equalize the position of all of us. I wonder if that principle were applied to the western farmer where we would be. Supposing we tried to place the western farmer in as good a position in regard to the world markets as is the eastern farmer? The member for Brome asked me a little while ago1 wherein our principles differ. I should like to put that proposition to him. Will he admit its soundness? Its application would mean the elimination of freight rates entirely as far as payment by the west is concerned.

subsubtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, 1919
speechtext:
It might. But I
imagine some eastern people would be very loath to admit a principle of that kind. To a very considerable extent we have admitted that principle in dealing with our postal rates, and I can send a letter three thousand miles for exactly the same charge as I can send another letter a mile. I am

not going to urge that this principle should be applied in this particular case, because there are a great many other factors entering into it-for instance, some people think we have better land in the west-but I would urge that this question of geographical location cannot be ignored, and that behind the plea that is frequently made, "In the east you have water competition," there lies this further geographical fact, that the industry of the west is almost entirely built up on our transportation system, and that unless we have that transportation system arranged on such a basis that it is possible for the west to produce at a reasonable cost, the west will be unable to carry on.
The right hon. leader of the opposition spoke against special privilege. He suggested1 that the west claimed special privileges. Again let me refer to my illustration of the payment of the transportation expenses of the members of this House. Would anyone seriously claim that because the member for Skeena is paid say $100 for his transportation expenses and the member for, say George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) $5, that there is a case of gross discrimination, a case of special privilege? I think not. The fact is that by paying one member much more than the other we are simply bringing about a measure of equality. These are some of the principles that underlie this very complicated question that we have before us. We have heard the appeal made again and again in this House that the freight rates must permit the railways to live. I should like to place side by side with that, this plea, that the freight rates must permit the west to live. This is all we ask. Let me say that I do not think that the majority of the members of this House, even although we have been trying to make out our case here during the last four yearn, yet realize the serious situation that exists in the west.

speechtext:
Let me review very briefly the situation as it appeals to some of us who make no claim whatever to being experts in this field.
The Crowsnest agreement we regard as a contract. I think that is admitted. The underlying principle is that of safeguarding the west iby maximum rates. The courts have decided that the agreement stands, but have robbed it of value. It is the duty of the highest court, the parliament of Canada, to give effect to the underlying principle. I do not know that I need to enlarge upon that statement. We are not insisting upon the agreement, according to strict legal interpretation, being maintained. We recognize that the situation is absolutely anomalous, that there must be changes, but we do say that parliament, as the highest court of this country, ought to give effect to the underlying principle, that of safeguarding the west by maximum rates. I quite agree that parliament is not the body to erect a freight rate structure. Any of us who has even glanced over the schedules realizes the difficulties, and these have been pointed out at length to this House, but I would urge that it is the duty of parliament to decide on basic principles.
The proposed legislation concedes part of the agreement. Why not the whole? It is all very well for the member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) to admit generously that he is not quite consistent in conceding a part, but I submit that underneath that admission, there is more or less a recognition of the real difficulties which are inherent in the situation, and the concession is in reality a concession to certain rights that ought to be recognized. The only reason given by the Minister of Railways for the rejection of the recognition of the whole principle is that the revenues of

Railway Freight Rates
the railroad would not stand it. He offers no figures in substantiation, and, more serious still, he offers no alternative.
I would submit, Mr. Chairman, that there are alternatives. Sooner or later we must change the entire basis on which the revenues of the railways are collected. We all know something of the political jobbery, the incompetence and graft that have characterized the history of the construction of railways in Canada. I do not intend to go into this matter, but merely by way of illustration let me call attention to one or two facts as given us in the Drayton-Acworth report back in 1917:
The property investment of the Canadian Northern Railway system is stated in the balance sheet of June 30, 1916, at $494,112,489.34. This figure admittedly has been written up to include $100,000,000 of capital stock. And this stock, as we have already said, was issued without any cash consideration. We have endeavoured to ascertain the actual cost of the system. From the company's official reports and special statement supplied to us, we have ascertained that the maximum cash investment that can have been made in the property is $383,302,451.33.
Thus fictitious capital stock is made a charge upon production. One other statement with regard to the Canadian Pacific railway. Here is a summary of the government aid that has been granted to the Canadian Pacific railway:
Completed road and surveys cost the government	$37,785,320
Cash subsidies	 66,905,481
Lands sold	123,810,124
Total public assistance	 228,500.925
Company's valuation put on unsold lands.. 119,259,000

The public has very largely paid for the road, and then private enterprise demands dividends on government grants. It is possible, I urge, quite possible, that instead of saying that we will allow the railways to live, that is, to pay dividends on these huge sums, we might alter the whole basis on which we compute these dividends.
One other suggestion that I would offer in closing has been put forward on several occasions during this session of the House, and that is the amalgamation of the railways into one system. That, it would seem, is the only ultimate solution that lies before us. It is inevitable sooner or later; why 12 m. not face it? We are informed that during the first four months of this year the gross earnings of the Canadian Pacific railway dropped $6,000,000 as compared with the corresponding period of last year. The gross earnings of the Canadian National Railway dropped a similar amount, $6,000,000, over the gross earnings of
the corresponding period of last year. How long can this state of affairs continue? It is being kept going at the present time very largely at the expense of the producer of this country. The labour people are being taxed, the employees of the railroads are being taxed, but worse still they are being laid off in large numbers in order that the railroads may make any showing at all. I need not speak for the farmers and the business men. I repeat how long can this state of affairs continue. We propose by this bill to penalize still further the producers of the west and not only the primary producers but a large number of people engaged in the distributional system. In our city of Winnipeg we are a long way from the seaboard. We are-
